articles.title: Continuum architecture dynamics of vesicle tethering in exocytosis
articles.summary: Data from complementary imaging techniques were integrated into a model that resolves the dynamic exocyst ensemble and membrane architecture during exocytosis, an essential cellular pathway. Sec18 mediates the rate of exocytosis by disassembling the exocyst higher-order structure after vesicle fusion.
articles.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Download PDF Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • Correlative imaging time-resolved protein and membrane architectures in exocytosis • A ring-shaped higher-order structure of 7 exocysts expands to a stable 38 nm radius • Tethered vesicles undergo 3 metastable states at 27, 18, and 5 nm from the membrane • Sec18 mediates the initiation of exocytic events by recycling exocysts after fusion Summary Essential for eukaryotes, multiple copies of the exocyst complex tether each secretory vesicle to the plasma membrane (PM) in constitutive exocytosis. The exocyst higher-order structure (ExHOS) that coordinates the action of these multiple exocysts remains unexplored. We integrated particle tracking, super-resolution microscopy, and cryo-electron tomography to time-resolve the continuum conformational landscape of the ExHOS and to functionally annotate its different conformations. We found that 7 exocysts form a flexible ring-shaped ExHOS that tethers vesicles at <45 nm from the PM. The ExHOS rapidly expands while pulling the vesicle toward the PM in a stepwise mechanism comprising three metastable states at 27, 18, and 5 nm from the PM. After fusion, Sec18 mediates the disassembly of the stationary ExHOS, a function that controls the rate of exocytosis. By resolving biophysical principles in situ, we reconstructed the spatiotemporal dynamics of the multimeric architecture controlling vesicle tethering in exocytosis. Graphical abstract Keywords constitutive exocytosis exocyst vesicle tethering particle tracking single molecule localization microscopy cryo-electron tomography in situ structural biology Sec18 metastable states exocyst higher-order structure Introduction Constitutive exocytosis (hereafter exocytosis), the uninterrupted transport of secretory vesicles to and subsequent fusion with the plasma membrane (PM), is an essential cellular process for nearly all eukaryotes. Exocytosis is critical for the preservation of PM homeostasis, cell growth, and cell division. At the heart of this intricate process lies the tethering, a finely tuned event that is responsible for the specific docking of cargo-loaded vesicles with the target PM. The exocyst, a conserved heterooctameric protein complex, is the main component of tethering.1,2,3 Beyond its canonical role in exocytosis, the exocyst is involved in the secretion of exosomes4 and herpesviruses.5 Not limited to secretory processes, it is a key player in autophagy, host invasion by pathogens (e.g., Salmonella typhimurium),6,7,8 and it is both a pathogen target and an immune receptor in plants.9,10 Together, these roles highlight the exocyst’s central importance across diverse biological pathways in both biomedical and agricultural contexts. Exocyst function relies on its interplay with other proteins that actively regulate exocytosis. For example, exocyst function requires the interaction, at the vesicle surface, with the nucleotide guanosine triphosphatase Sec4 and its guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor Sec2.11,12 The exocyst also binds Sec9, a soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE). Exocyst-Sec9 interaction supports the exocytic trans-SNARE complex formation, which is critical for subsequent vesicle fusion.13 After cargo release, the AAA ATPase Sec18 hydrolyzes ATP and, together with the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein (α-SNAP) co-chaperone Sec17, it culminates the process of exocytosis by disassembling the cis-SNARE complex, which is recycled for the progression of a new round of tethering and fusion.14,15 In vitro experiments have been essential in providing high-resolution data on this tethering complex. The most complete structure of the isolated exocyst measures 32 nm long and 13 nm wide. Although this structure still lacks 18% of the complex, it has uncovered the atomic details that sustain the assembly of the octamer into two tetrameric modules: module I contains Sec3, Sec5, Sec6, and Sec8 subunits, while module II consists of Sec10, Sec15, Exo70, and Exo84 subunits.16,17 In vitro experiments also located the regions in Sec15 and Sec6 C termini that bind functional partners, such as Sec4-Sec2 and Sec9, respectively.17,18 However, in the cell, the tethering of a single vesicle involves multiple copies of the exocyst19,20,21 with defined stoichiometries and temporal correlation with its partners.19,21 Therefore, tethering is governed by a dynamic higher-order mechanism, which could not be reconstituted in vitro. In situ analysis of the higher-order mechanism of tethering is further complicated by the polarized and transient nature of the exocytic events, which tend to occur in highly localized regions of the PM.21 These challenges, combined with the intrinsic complexity and constitutive dynamism of exocytosis, have limited the quantitative studies of exocytosis under native conditions. Thus, the spatiotemporal organization of the multiple exocysts mediating vesicle tethering (the exocyst higher-order structure, hereafter named ExHOS), along with its functional annotation, remains an unresolved milestone in the field. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we integrated 2-color simultaneous particle tracking of exocytic proteins, super-resolution microscopy, and cryo-correlative light and electron microscopy (cryo-CLEM) to resolve the dynamic architecture of multiple exocysts and the secretory vesicle during exocytosis. Results Measuring the vesicle radius and the exocyst copy number to model the tethering Exocytosis inherently involves the interaction and shaping of membranes (secretory vesicles and PM). The combination of focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM)22 and cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET)23 offers an intimate 3D view of this membrane ultrastructure in vitrified cells. We imaged and segmented 175 vesicles adjacent (i.e., <70 nm of distance) to the PM of yeast cells (Figures 1A and S1A–S1C). Spherical vesicles, with an average radius of 41 ± 4 nm (mean ± SD), were located preferentially at distances below 45 nm from the PM (Figure 1A). This suggests the presence of an underlying mechanism that drives this proximal accumulation, such as exocyst-mediated tethering. Figure 1 Modeling the spatial arrangement of vesicle tethering Show full caption Figure S1 Workflow of vesicle-PM distance estimation, exocyst copy-number measurement, and modeling of ExHOS, related to Figure 1 Show full caption The first step in elucidating the higher-order mechanism of such vesicle tethering was to determine the stoichiometry of exocysts involved in this process, which remains inconclusive and incomplete for all exocyst subunits.19,20,21 We measured the average number of each subunit fused to GFP using a live-cell fluorescence intensity ratiometric assay,24 with Cse4-GFP as a reference (STAR Methods).25 In agreement with the number of Sec3, Sec5, Sec6, Sec8, and Exo70 subunits found in exocyst clusters of mammalian cells,19 we found that 7 ± 1 (mean ± pooled SEM) exocysts are present at exocytic events, on average, with the expected 1 to 1 stoichiometry for all the subunits (Figures 1B and S1D). Subsequently, we investigated how 6–8 exocysts can tether vesicles of 41 nm in radius situated at different distances from the PM. To address this question, we modeled the possible conformational space of the ExHOS that can bind the vesicle and the PM simultaneously (Figures 1C and S1E; STAR Methods). Each exocyst was represented as a cylinder of 13 nm diameter and 32 nm height. The radial location of a given exocyst ( 𝜌 ), which is the distance of the exocyst centroid to the central axis in the vesicle-PM interface, was used henceforth as a descriptor of the ExHOS (Figure 1C). Given the fixed length of the exocyst in our model, 𝜌 depends on the vesicle-PM distance ( 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 in Figure 1C) and the conformation that the exocyst adopts in relation to the PM plane. The conformational relationship among the multiple exocysts involved in the ExHOS imposes two plausible architectural modalities linked to different mechanisms of tethering. A first mechanism, where the multiple exocysts tethering a vesicle adopt heterotypic conformations, would allow the 6–8 exocysts to be unevenly dispersed along a patch-shaped ExHOS between the vesicle and the PM. Hence, exocyst positions could range from a 𝜌 of nearly 6.5 nm, corresponding to the cylinder radius, to 50 nm (Figure 1D, left). A second mechanism is also plausible, where all the exocysts within an ExHOS adopt a homotypic conformation. By requiring that the exocysts adopt the same conformation relative to the vesicle and the PM, ring-shaped models are obtained, where all exocysts share the same 𝜌 value (hereafter, ExHOS radius) (Figure 1D, right). The radius of the ring-shaped ExHOS depends on the number of complexes that must be accommodated and the distance at which the vesicle is tethered to the PM (Figure S1F). Thus, the theoretical ExHOS with 6 exocysts tethering the vesicle at 34 nm from the PM has a radius of 15 nm, while the ExHOS tethering the vesicle at 4 nm from the PM has a radius of up to 50 nm (Figure 1D, right). The biological relevance of both mechanisms might be related with the distribution of forces exerted by the exocysts to control the lateral diffusion of the vesicle. In this context, ring-shaped ExHOS are more likely to provide isotropic lateral forces that could result in a vesicle displacement orthogonal to the PM in preparation for the subsequent fusion. Exocysts organize in ring-like higher-order structures with variable radius To experimentally assess the ExHOS organization in situ, we used single molecule localization microscopy (SMLM),26 a light microscopy technique that provides ∼20 nm resolution. We imaged fixed cells endogenously expressing exocyst subunits Sec5, Sec6, and Sec8, from module I, fused to the photoswitchable fluorescent protein mMaple (mM), and Exo84, from module II, fused to GFP (exocyst-mM-GFP). We obtained two-dimensional projections of exocyst-mM-GFP clusters by setting the focal plane at the bottom of the cells (Figure 2A). Correlating SMLM and diffraction-limited wide-field microscopy (DL) images allowed us to segment 136 individual exocyst-mM-GFP clusters (Figure 2A). Due to its sensitivity and resolution, SMLM is a robust approach to quantify the average copy number in protein clusters.25,27 Consistent with the live-cell fluorescence intensity ratiometric assay, on average, 5.8 ± 3.4 exocysts populate exocyst-mM-GFP clusters (Figures 2A and S2). Figure 2 Structural analysis of the ExHOS by SMLM Show full caption Figure S2 Quantification of exocyst copy number in SMLM datasets, related to Figures 2, 4, and 5 Show full caption The sparsity of exocysts populating ExHOS makes its structural analysis by SMLM highly sensitive to the uneven photoconversion of mM molecules and its limited labeling efficiency.28 Nonetheless, in agreement with a homotypic exocyst conformation in ExHOS, visual inspection identified ring-like shapes in some of the exocyst-mM-GFP cluster images (Figure 2A). To tackle the conundrum of the ExHOS shape more systematically, we compiled a synthetic dataset of the expected SMLM images resulting from imaging exocyst-mM clusters where the multiple exocysts follow heterotypic (i.e., patch-like) or homotypic (i.e., ring-like) ExHOS. We considered radii between 20 and 50 nm (STAR Methods). We then compared the gyration radius, a measure of dispersion (STAR Methods), of the localizations observed in the experimental dataset, with the gyration radius of the simulated data. Interestingly, only the synthetic dataset of ring-shaped ExHOS could recapitulate the localizations’ gyration radius above 70 nm observed experimentally (Figure 2B). In addition, the simulations also indicate that the coexistence of ring-shaped ExHOS with different radii is necessary to fully explain the broad range of localizations’ gyration radius observed experimentally. Cryo-ET data, computational predictions, and SMLM-DL imaging imply that 7 exocysts on average can arrange in a ring-shaped ExHOS that adopts different radii on the cellular PM. However, it remains unclear if the ExHOS assortment is simply the result of stochasticity or if it is rooted in the observation, at distinct time points, of a regulated dynamic mechanism. A map of the exocytic machinery dynamism serves as a time ruler of exocytosis To investigate the temporal control of ExHOS, we explored the temporal correlation of exocyst clusters with other proteins of the exocytic machinery. We first used the live-cell fluorescence intensity ratiometric assay24 to estimate the stoichiometry in PM-associated clusters of proteins representative of the main functional steps of exocytosis: Sec2-mNeonGreen (Sec2-mNG) (vesicle transport), mNG-Sec9 (vesicle fusion), and Sec18-mNG (protein recycling). We found that, on average, each exocytic event consists of 8 ± 1, 9 ± 1, and 37 ± 5 copies of Sec2-mNG, mNG-Sec9, and Sec18-mNG, respectively (Figure S3A), which is consistent with a ∼1:1 stoichiometry between the exocyst and Sec2, Sec9, and the Sec17-Sec18 complex (which is formed by 4 copies of Sec17 and 6 copies of Sec18).29,30,31 Figure S3 Quantification of copy numbers within Sec2-mNG, mNG-Sec9, and Sec18-mNG clusters and colocalization with Exo84-mCh clusters, related to Figure 3 Show full caption Live-cell imaging also allowed us to quantify, with 115–120 ms temporal resolution, the dynamics of these proteins during exocytic events. We performed simultaneous two-color diffraction-limited imaging at the equatorial plane of yeast cells expressing Exo84 fused to mCherry (exocyst-mCh) and a mNG-tagged marker (Sec2-mNG, mNG-Sec9, or Sec18-mNG; Figure 3A; STAR Methods). Particle tracking of 90 exocytic events allowed us to quantify the average dynamics of mNG-tagged markers in relation to the average intensity profile along the lifetime of exocyst-mCh clusters (Figure 3B; STAR Methods). Under our experimental conditions, exocyst-mCh clusters present an average lifetime of 9.4 ± 0.5 s (Figure 3C). Underscoring the functional relevance of filtered tracks, more than 90% of the exocyst-mCh clusters colocalize with clusters of mNG-tagged markers (Figure S3B), including the recruitment of Sec18-mNG, which we use as a proxy of the normal termination of exocytosis after vesicle fusion. In addition, 90% of the Sec2-mNG clusters immobilized to the PM coincide in time and space with the detection of immobile exocyst-mCh clusters. Overall, this demonstrates that the majority of exocyst-mCh clusters tracked by our approach correspond to functional individual events of exocytosis. Figure 3 Dynamics of exocytic events Show full caption All the mNG-tagged marker tracks were aligned to the release time of the exocyst-mCh clusters, normalized by their corresponding maximum corrected intensity, and then averaged. The detection of Sec2-mNG tracks is concomitant with the clustering of exocyst-mCh, which we interpret as tethering initiation. Then, the soluble SNARE mNG-Sec9 is recruited to exocytic events 3.1 ± 0.2 s after the clustering of exocyst-mCh. Sec2-mNG and mNG-Sec9 concur in the event of exocytosis for about 5.5 s. Subsequently, Sec2-mNG is released 0.8 ± 0.6 s before the release of exocyst-mCh clusters. Finally, Sec18-mNG is recruited to exocytic events 9.1 ± 0.5 s after tethering started, yielding a short, yet consistent, 0.3 s colocalization with the exocyst-mCh on average (Figures 3B and 3C). The signal of mNG-Sec9 and Sec18-mNG clusters at the exocytic event disappears 2.5 ± 0.1 and 4.3 ± 0.1 s after the release of exocyst-mCh clusters, respectively. Overall, from the biogenesis of static exocyst-mCh clusters associated with the PM to the release of Sec18-mNG, the process of exocytosis lasts 13.7 ± 0.6 s, on average. The reported temporal map indicates that the presence of different fluorescent markers defines overlapping but distinct time windows along the exocyst-mCh cluster lifetime: Sec2 (0–8.6 s), Sec9 (3.1–9.4 s), and Sec18 (9.1–9.4 s) (Figure 3C). These time windows allowed us to address the temporal organization of the ExHOS. The ring-shaped ExHOS follows a radial expansion during exocytosis Equipped with temporal markers, we next investigated the existence of a dynamic ring-shaped ExHOS that adjusts its radius to suit the tethering of the secretory vesicle as it approaches the PM. Unfortunately, it is not possible to continuously follow the structural dynamics of the ExHOS in the cell because of the technical limitations of SMLM. Instead, we correlated SMLM imaging of exocyst-mM with DL imaging of the temporal markers Sec2-GFP and mNG-Sec9. For each dataset, we computed the average image (STAR Methods). In agreement with a structurally dynamic ExHOS, exocyst-mM clusters that colocalize with Sec2-GFP present a patch-shaped average image, with a radius of 32 ± 2 nm, while those that colocalize with mNG-Sec9 present a ring-shaped average image with a 37 ± 1 nm radius (Figure 4A; STAR Methods). Figure 4 The conformational dynamics of the ExHOS time-resolved by SMLM Show full caption To estimate the underlying continuum dynamics of the ExHOS, we first discriminated between the two conformational extremes predicted by computational models. According to the modeled ExHOS that contains 6–8 homotypic exocysts (Figure 1D, right), the ExHOS radius varies between 15 and 22 nm (defined here as the compact ExHOS class) for the tethering at 32–34 nm from the PM. Instead, ExHOS radius can fluctuate between 28 and 50 nm (defined here as the expanded ExHOS class) for the tethering at 4 nm from the PM (Figure 4B). We used the synthetic dataset of ring-shaped ExHOS to train a random forest classifier to systematically classify the imaged exocyst-mM-GFP clusters according to their likelihood of representing a compact or an expanded ExHOS. The classifier achieved 90% accuracy in classifying synthetic SMLM images (Figures 4C and S4A; STAR Methods). Figure S4 Training workflow for the random forest classifier of exocyst clusters imaged by SMLM and their subsequent characterization, related to Figures 4 and 5 Show full caption Overall, 27% ± 3% and 73% ± 6% of the exocyst-mM clusters correlating with Sec2-GFP were classified as compact and expanded ExHOS, respectively (Figures 4D and S4B). In line with our models, and considering the ∼20 nm resolution of SMLM, the average compact ExHOS appears as a patch-shaped cluster, with an estimated radius of 19 ± 1 nm. The average expanded ExHOS presents a wider ring-like shape, with an estimated radius of 36 ± 1 nm (Figures S4C and S4D; STAR Methods). However, only 9% ± 4% of the exocyst-mM clusters correlating with mNG-Sec9 were predicted to follow a compact ExHOS, whereas 91% ± 4% of them were classified as expanded (Figures 4D and S4B). The average image for expanded clusters colocalizing with mNG-Sec9 presents a ring with fewer localizations in the center, which results in a significantly larger radius (38 ± 1 nm; Figures S4C and S4D). We could not detect any significant difference in the number of exocysts populating the cluster at each time window (Figures 4A and S2B). In conclusion, the combination of SMLM and fluorescent temporal markers shows that clusters of 7 exocysts, on average, transition from compact to expanded ExHOS along the process of exocytosis. The description of the ExHOS dynamics presented until this point is based on the idea of two well-defined conformations: compact and expanded. This approximation of the realistic continuous tethering mechanism to two discrete conformations allowed us to question if a switch from a compact to an expanded ExHOS could be explained by a structural transition following first-order reaction-like kinetics: 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 = exp ( − 𝑘 ∗ 𝑡 ) , (Equation 1) where 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 is the relative population of the compact class. The average rate constant 𝑘 was estimated based on the fraction of compact and expanded ExHOS present in the Sec2 time window: 𝑘 = 0.38 ± 0.06 s−1 (Figure 4D; STAR Methods). Underscoring the relevance of the model, the estimated rate constant could predict the fraction of compact and expanded ExHOS measured in the Sec9 time window (Figure 4D). Consequently, this model allowed us to predict the continuous ExHOS conformational dynamics (i.e., the average ExHOS radius, 𝑟 𝐸 𝑥 𝐻 𝑂 𝑆 , along the lifetime of exocyst clusters; Figure 4E): 𝑟 𝐸 𝑥 𝐻 𝑂 𝑆 ( 𝑡 ) = 39.0 − 20.5 ∗ exp ( − 0.38 ∗ 𝑡 ) [ 𝑛 𝑚 ] . (Equation 2) According to this model, the ExHOS initiates, on average, as an ∼19 nm radius ring and undergoes an exponential radial expansion with a mean half-lifetime of ∼3 s. To challenge this model derived from the Sec2-GFP dataset, we computed the integrated average radius for the ExHOS corresponding to the Sec9 time window. In agreement with Equation 2, the average radius measured for the exocyst-mM clusters that correlate with mNG-Sec9 (37 ± 1 nm) matches the predicted average radius (37 ± 1 nm) (Figure 4E). Remarkably, the model predicts a stationary conformation of the ExHOS 9.4 s after tethering initiation, with an average radius of 39 ± 1 nm (Figure 4E). Unfortunately, the inherent short-lived colocalization between the exocyst and Sec18 precluded us from obtaining sufficient data to resolve the ExHOS during the last 300 ms of the exocyst cluster lifetime. Sec18 is required for the disassembly of stationary ExHOS and it controls the initiation of new exocytic events To challenge the theoretical stability of the ExHOS at the final stages of exocytosis, we investigated the molecular basis that regulates the release of exocyst clusters. Interestingly, the average intensity profile shows that the release of exocyst-mCh clusters progresses in parallel to the clustering of Sec18-mNG (Figure 3B). Moreover, the correlation (r = 0.84) between the release of exocyst-mCh clusters and the start of Sec18-mNG clustering (Figure S5A, left) underscores the relevance that Sec18 might have, directly or indirectly, in controlling the dynamics of the ExHOS. In contrast, the clustering (Figure S5A, left) and the release (Figure S5A, right) of mNG-Sec9 and Sec2-mNG show moderate or no correlation with exocyst-mCh release. Therefore, Sec18 arises as the most plausible protein that might be involved in the release and recycling of exocyst clusters. Figure S5 Characterization of cells depleted of Sec18-FRB, related to Figure 5 Show full caption To study the functional relevance of this AAA ATPase, we engineered cells for the inducible depletion of Sec18 using the anchor-away approach32 (Figures 5A and S5B; STAR Methods). Importantly, as the different vesicle transport pathways participated in by the AAA ATPase are interconnected, impairing Sec18 function is likely to eventually impact all these pathways with little specificity. To avoid the general collapse of vesicle transport, we engineered cells for partial depletion of Sec18 tagged to FKBP-rapamycin-binding (FRB) domain (Sec18-FRB) to specifically investigate the role of Sec18 in the dynamics of the ExHOS (Figures S5C–S5F; STAR Methods). Figure 5 Sec18 is necessary for the disassembly of the ExHOS and the initiation of exocytic events Show full caption First, we measured the dynamics of exocyst-mCh and mNG-Sec9 clusters upon the depletion of Sec18-FRB. As anticipated, cells depleted for Sec18-FRB accumulate mNG-Sec9 at the PM in clusters that increase their lifetime 2.5-fold (Figure 5B). In agreement with an additional role of the AAA ATPase in the recycling of the ExHOS, cells depleted for Sec18-FRB accumulate exocyst-mCh clusters, whose lifetime increases 2.3-fold (Figure 5B). These increments in lifetimes are necessarily underestimated due to the difficulty in capturing longer tracks within limited imaging times. We then imaged exocyst-mM-mNG clusters by SMLM-DL upon Sec18-FRB depletion. In agreement with the continuous ExHOS conformational dynamics model (Figures 4D and 4E), nearly all the ExHOS in cells depleted for Sec18-FRB were classified as expanded ExHOS (94% ± 4%; Figure S4B), and the average image presents a ring-like shape with an average radius of 38 ± 1 nm (Figures 5C, S4C, and S4D). Overall, our results indicate that Sec18 is required for the native disassembly of ring-shaped ExHOS during the last 300 ms of the exocyst cluster’s lifetime, when they have a stationary radius of around 38 nm, on average. As Sec18 recycles SNAREs after each fusion event,14,15 it is plausible that ExHOS disassembly is non-specifically caused by steric hindrances resulting from the recruitment of Sec18 to the cis-SNARE complex. On the other hand, a targeted interaction between the exocyst and Sec18 might exist independently of the cis-SNARE complex. To investigate the mode of ExHOS disassembly, we used PICT (protein interactions from imaging complexes after translocation33), a live-cell imaging technique to detect protein-protein interactions. In our PICT assay, direct and indirect interactions are measured as a change in the localization of Sec18-mNG upon the inducible anchoring of the exocyst subunit Sec15-FRB to anchoring platforms (STAR Methods). Sec15-FRB anchoring recruits the full exocyst bound to the secretory vesicle, which cannot undergo fusion due to the separation of the anchoring platform from the PM.20 Nonetheless, the recruitment score of Sec18-mNG to the anchoring platform increased 1.5-fold upon Sec15-FRB anchoring (Figure S5G). This indicates that there is a targeted interaction—either direct or indirect—between the exocyst and Sec18, which does not require the formation of the cis-SNARE complex. To systematically assess the proximity and hierarchy of Sec18 interactions with SNAREs and the exocyst, we carried out affinity purification-mass spectrometry (AP-MS) with cross-linking experiments (STAR Methods). We performed a partial cross-linking to detect proximal peptides in cell extracts.34 As expected, Exo84-GFP pull-down retrieved all the exocyst subunits (Sec5 is shown for illustrative purposes in Figure 5D). In agreement with the PICT assay, we also detected Sec18 in Exo84-GFP pull-down before Sec18-FRB depletion, while the sequestration of Sec18-FRB prevented the interaction with the exocyst subunit (Figure 5D). In comparison, we were unable to detect Sec9 and Sec17 under any condition. Indeed, the depletion of FRB-Sec9 did not impact the detected Exo84-Sec18 interaction, suggesting that the cis-SNARE complex is not required for that interaction (Figure S5H). The specificity of the interactions found is further supported by AP-MS experiments performed with cells expressing Exo84 lacking the GFP tag (Figure 5D). Thus, AP-MS together with inducible depletion demonstrated that Exo84 and Sec18 interact in close proximity and that this interaction does not require the SNARE Sec9. Our results suggest that Sec18 might be necessary to preserve the reservoir of active exocyst by disassembling the ExHOS. Importantly, the cytosolic levels of Exo84-mNG are 40% lower than the cytosolic levels of mNG-Sec9 (Figure 5E), suggesting that exocyst recycling, rather than SNAREs recycling, is the limiting factor to preserve the native rates of new exocytic events. Thus, our results pose a conundrum regarding the hierarchy of the AAA ATPase functions in exocytosis. To investigate the relevance of Sec18-mediated ExHOS disassembly, we quantified the performance of exocyst and Sec9 clusters by particle tracking upon partial depletion of Sec18. Upon 15 min of depletion, the rate of formation of exocyst-mNG clusters decreased 47% (Figure 5F). Instead, in those events of exocytosis that did initiate, we could not detect any significant decrease in the engagement of mNG-Sec9 (Figure 5G). Furthermore, this partial depletion of Sec18 over a longer timescale resulted in a 42% inhibition of the secretion of Bgl2, a cargo of exocytosis (Figure 5H). Overall, this indicates that, under our experimental conditions, Sec18 controls the rate of exocytosis by regulating the recycling of exocysts rather than the disassembly of the cis-SNARE complex. The ultrastructure associated with exocyst clusters: From tethering to fusion To complement the continuous ExHOS conformational dynamics with defined functional annotations, we used cryo-CLEM to resolve the ultrastructure of the participating membranes. We took advantage of the fluorescent temporal markers to experimentally time-resolve the vesicle distance to the PM. We first imaged cells endogenously expressing the exocyst subunits Sec5, Exo70, and Exo84 fused to mNG (exocyst-mNG; Figure 6A). We acquired and reconstructed a dataset of 95 tomograms correlated with diffraction-limited exocyst-mNG clusters (STAR Methods). In 76 cases, we could unambiguously correlate the presence of an isolated vesicle with the exocyst-mNG cluster (i.e., no other tethered vesicle could be observed at a distance <250 nm). While tomography data show irregular densities at the interstitial area between each vesicle and the PM, a quantitative analysis based on subtomogram averaging of such areas was not feasible (STAR Methods). In the other 19 tomograms, no vesicle or PM deformations were detected (Figure 6A). We also performed cryo-CLEM on cells expressing Sec9 fused to mScarlet3 (mSc3-Sec9) to question whether vesicles can be temporally aligned based on their separation from the PM (Figure 6B). We targeted the acquisition of fourteen tomograms to mSc3-Sec9 diffraction-limited clusters, and in five of those tomograms, we could unambiguously correlate an isolated vesicle. In the remaining nine tomograms, no vesicle or PM deformations could be correlated (Figure 6B). We did not image cells expressing Sec2-mNG because this marker alone cannot distinguish tethered from non-tethered vesicles in vitrified samples. Interestingly, while exocyst-mNG-correlated vesicles display a wide spectrum of distances to the PM (i.e., from 2 to ∼43 nm), all vesicles found within the Sec9 time window lay closer than 7 nm from the PM (Figure 6C; Table S1). Figure 6 Time-resolved ultrastructure of the tethering Show full caption Importantly, as Sec18 is known to be recruited to the exocytic cis-SNARE complex after vesicle fusion,15,35 the coincidence of Sec18-mNG and exocyst-mCh suggests that the ExHOS might have a role related to vesicle fusion, in line with recently published in vitro reconstitutions.36 Remarkably, in 19 out of 95 tomograms targeted to exocyst-mNG clusters (20%) and in 9 of the 14 tomograms targeted to mSc3-Sec9 clusters (64%), we could not find any nearby vesicle or PM deformation (Figures 6A and 6B). Although we could not capture fusion intermediates, our tomograms suggest that the vesicle and the PM fuse in a rapid and transient event, in agreement with experiments showing that multiple exocysts promote vesicle full fusion with the PM.37 Hence, combining cryo-CLEM with the relative lifetime of the exocyst-mCh cluster (Figures 3B and 3C), we estimated that 7.5 s after tethering initiation, the vesicle fuses with the PM in the presence of the ExHOS (STAR Methods). This estimation is in agreement with the larger fraction of the tomograms targeted to mSc3-Sec9 clusters that are devoid of vesicles (Figure 6B). Overall, the integration of SMLM-DL, genetics, and cryo-CLEM implies that, as tethering progresses, the vesicle is unidirectionally dragged toward the PM. Upon fusion, the ExHOS preserves its conformation on the PM for nearly 2 s, despite the lack of a vesicle that scaffolds the ring-shaped conformation. The time-resolved ultrastructure reveals a stepwise tethering mechanism To experimentally determine the dynamism and membrane plasticity involved in secretory vesicle tethering, we utilized the distribution of the closest distance to the PM and the sphericity for each vesicle, correlated with exocyst-mNG (Figures 6C, S6A, and S6B). Our measurements show that tethered vesicles do not distribute evenly from the PM. Instead, 95% of the tethered vesicles accumulate within distance ranges that are compatible with three metastable states (i.e., MS1–3): MS1 harbors 15% of the vesicles at a mean distance of 27 ± 1.4 nm, MS2 harbors 42% of the vesicles at a mean distance of 18 ± 2.8 nm, and MS3 harbors 38% of the tethered vesicles at a mean distance of 5 ± 2.7 nm. Instead, all vesicles correlating with mSc3-Sec9 are separated from the PM by a distance that coincides with MS3 (Figure 6C). We could not detect any deviation from ideal sphericity of the vesicles populating MS1, MS2, and MS3 (Figures S6A and S6B; STAR Methods). Figure S6 Characterization of protein dynamics and ultrastructure of MS1, MS2, and MS3, related to Figure 6 Show full caption Following this, we temporally ordered the distances between tethered vesicles and the PM (Figure 6D). This allowed us to use cryo-CLEM to estimate the vesicle kinetics toward the PM throughout the lifespan of exocyst clusters. During tethering, the vesicle follows three main displacement steps toward the PM: step 1, the fastest displacement, brings the vesicle from the initiation of tethering at 43 nm from the PM to MS1. In step 2, with the smallest approximation to the PM, the vesicle is transferred from MS1 to MS2. Finally, in step 3, the vesicle is carried from MS2 to MS3. Ultimately, the vesicle fuses with the PM ∼7.5 s after the initiation of vesicle tethering, on average (Figure 6D; STAR Methods). Overall, time-ordering the ultrastructure associated with exocyst clusters revealed that tethering consists of 3 main metastable states at around 27, 18, and 5 nm from the PM. Such a non-continuous movement necessarily originates from different molecular functions that act sequentially and that control the kinetics of approximation of the vesicle to the PM in a stepwise mechanism. Investigating the interaction between lipids and proteins regulating exocyst function, such as PI(4,5)P2,38 Boi1/2,39,40 Sro7,41 Rho3, and Cdc42,42,43 might shed light on this mechanism. Sec1 binds both exocyst and SNAREs, and genetic experiments have shown that it plays a critical role in promoting the trans-SNARE complex formation.44 Particle tracking shows that mNG-Sec1 clusters to exocytic events when vesicles are at MS2 (simultaneously to mNG-Sec9 clustering), but it releases together with the exocyst (Figure S6C). This agrees with a mechanism where the recruitment of Sec1 induces a structural switch that promotes the assembly of the trans-SNARE complex and the subsequent transition of the vesicle from MS2 to MS3. Regarding Sec1 release from exocytic events, the depletion of Sec18-FRB resulted in a 2.5-fold increase in the lifetime of mNG-Sec1 clusters (Figure S6D), suggesting that Sec1’s concomitant departure with exocyst might also be Sec18-mediated. Further experiments will be required to pinpoint the molecules responsible and the conformational changes associated with the transition between metastable states, which remains a major gap in our understanding of the mechanism of exocytosis. A model integrating time-resolved architecture with functional annotation of the ExHOS The quantitative characterization of fluorescent temporal markers endowed the synergy between SMLM-DL and cryo-CLEM, allowing us to reconstruct the time-resolved architecture of tethering, including its structural dynamics and functional annotation, in an integrative model (Figure 7; Video S1). Accordingly, tethering initiates when a cluster of 7 ± 1 exocysts arranges in a ring-shaped ExHOS with an average radius of 19 nm. During step 1, the ExHOS radially expands while it quickly pulls the vesicle toward the PM until it reaches MS1, at 27 nm from the PM. MS1 is the most transient of the metastable states and is mediated by an expanding ExHOS of 25 nm in radius, on average. In step 2, the vesicle is pulled to MS2, where an ExHOS of 33 nm in radius, on average, holds the vesicle for more than 2 s. After clustering of Sec9 and, presumably, the incipient zippering of the trans-SNARE complex, the vesicle undergoes step 3 to reach MS3, where the ExHOS locks the vesicle at a distance of ∼5 nm from the PM. This metastable state is controlled by a stationary ExHOS with an average radius of 37 nm. In this conformation, the exocyst is likely to coexist with the trans-SNARE complex (fully or partially zippered), as the distance between vesicle-associated SNAREs and SNAREs integral to the PM would allow the complex formation (Figure S7A). Upon vesicle fusion with the PM, the stationary ExHOS, with an average radius of 38 nm, remains associated with the PM for 1.9 s. Eventually, the ExHOS is disassembled by an unknown reaction that requires Sec18. This disassembly of ExHOS is necessary to preserve the native rate of exocytosis events, likely by recycling exocysts so that they can engage in new cycles of tethering. Discussion Complementary imaging and modeling allowed us to resolve the native choreography of the ExHOS and cellular membranes during exocytosis. The stoichiometry and plasticity of the ExHOS within a stepwise tethering mechanism We showed that, on average, 7 exocysts organize in a ring-shaped ExHOS to control vesicle tethering. The number of exocysts is remarkably similar to the Munc13 hexamers that have been proposed to control mammalian synaptic exocytosis,45,46 however, the radius of synaptic vesicles is nearly half as compared with those of secretory vesicles in yeast.47 The similarity in the stoichiometry of related—yet evolutionarily distant—pathways suggests that the number of exocysts might be critical for their function, such as the lateral immobilization of the tethered vesicle. Integrative modeling provides mechanistic clues on tethering initiation Although tethering starts when the vesicle is at ∼45 nm from the PM (Figure 6D), the dimensions of the exocyst structure in isolation cannot account for such a distance (Figure 7; Video S1). Instead, our reconstruction of the initial tethering hypothesizes that the extension of the Sec3’s N terminus (residues 250–611 that were not resolved by cryo-EM) might be critical to determine the longest distance at which vesicles can be tethered (Figure S7B). Indeed, this flexible stretch can link the exocyst with the Sec3 pleckstrin-homology (PH) domain that targets the complex to the PM18 for up to 126 nm (in an ideal full extension). Interestingly, Sec3’s N terminus contains 24 phosphorylation sites, which have been suggested to regulate Sec3 folding and binding to partners.18 The post-translational modification of Sec3’s N terminus would provide a fast mechanism for the regulation of vesicle kinetics along step 1. The role of SNAREs in a stepwise tethering mechanism The coincidence of MS2, step 3, and MS3 with Sec9 and Sec1 clusters opens the possibility that the formation of the trans-SNARE complex plays a role in the stepwise mechanism. Supporting this idea, structural modeling shows that yeast exocytic SNAREs associated with the vesicle and the PM can only start zippering when the two membranes are found at distances under 24 nm (Figure S7C). While first interactions between SNAREs may happen in MS2, the proximity between membranes in step 3 and MS3 suggests that the vesicle displacement involves the zippering of the trans-SNARE complex. Interestingly, reconstitution of vesicle tethering with the isolated human exocyst detected distal tethering (32.1 nm) but could not recapitulate proximal tethering observed in MS2 and MS3,48 further supporting an essential role of the SNAREs in the confinement of secretory vesicles at 18 and 5 nm from the PM. Sec18 promotes ExHOS disassembly to preserve the rate of exocytosis After fusion, the stationary ExHOS, with a radius of 38 nm, remains associated with the PM for 1.9 s. Here, we have shown that Sec18 is required for the native disassembly of ExHOS (Figure 5). Unexpectedly, upon partial depletion of functional Sec18, we could not detect a defect in mNG-Sec9 activation, whose capacity to cluster in exocytic events remained unimpaired (Figure 5G). Instead, the rate of clustering of exocyst-mCh and Bgl2 secretion dropped by more than 40% (Figures 5F and 5H), indicating that the initiation of new exocytic events is limited by the recycling of exocysts rather than the recycling of SNAREs. Thus, our results underscore the functional relevance of ExHOS disassembly: a mechanism that ensures new secretory vesicles are only engaged for tethering if ongoing exocytic events are terminating normally. Although we showed that Exo84 and Sec18 interact in close proximity, the mechanism used by Sec18 to disassemble ExHOS remains unknown. It is unlikely that exocyst release involves the hydrolysis of ATP, as the unwinding of the cis-SNARE complex, known to involve this activity,15 occurs 2.5 s later (Figures 3B and 3C). Indeed, mNG-Sec9 release poorly correlates with exocyst release (r = −0.21), suggesting that ATPase activity is not involved in the disassembly of ExHOS. Instead, we hypothesize that ATP binding by the D2 domain of Sec18 or the action of Sec17 (or other unknown proteins) would provide the energy required to disassemble the ExHOS. Unfortunately, our attempts to resolve this mechanism by using Sec18 mutants or Sec17 constructs resulted in major defects of the exocyst subcellular distribution that prevented us from deriving meaningful data. Overall, this study provides quantitative insights into the biophysical principles that drive tethering of secretory vesicles. Given the exocyst’s central role across multiple cellular processes and diseases, these insights could help advance our understanding of the exocyst’s mechanism of action across biology more generally. Limitations of the study Capturing mechanistic nuances, such as reversibility in dynamics or biological heterogeneity, remains unattainable because of the need for averaging. For example, while the average copy of exocyst subunits is highly homotypic, the exocyst clusters show a broad distribution of brightness and lifetime that suggests larger differences among individual events (Figures 3C and S1D). Although ring-shaped ExHOS suggest a homotypic conformation of the multiple exocysts, no current technique can experimentally resolve individual exocysts. Despite calibration, the estimated radius of ExHOS may have a few nm offsets because SMLM localizes fluorescent tags. Along these lines, the variance in the size and tethering distance of vesicles imaged by cryo-CLEM prevented subtomogram averaging of proteins captured in expectably different conformational states, necessary to adapt to the different geometries found in situ. Resolving how the continuum landscape of ExHOS conformations is linked to the kinetics of the tethered vesicle opens up an avenue for understanding the mechanism of the exocytic machinery as an ensemble. We forecast that the continuum dynamics of proteinaceous higher-order structures and membrane deformation kinetics will be central in the study of other pathways in membrane biology. BY4742 backgrounds. A complete list of the strains used in this study can be found in Table S2 and protocols for strain generations are described below. Unless otherwise indicated, yeast cells were inoculated from single colonies in 3 mL of YPD and grown overnight at 30 °C. The next morning, saturated cultures were diluted in yeast extract peptone dextrose (YPD) or low-fluorescence media and grown for a minimum of 5 h until they reached OD600 of 0.8-1. Method details Yeast strain generation Standard PCR-based genetic manipulation methods were used to generate strains with C-terminally tagged proteins.49 Shortly, a DNA cassette containing the tag followed by a selectable marker was amplified using oligos that matched the C-terminal end of the desired protein. This cassette was inserted into the parental stain and transformed colonies were selected according to the proper selection marker. Seamless N-terminal tagging was done as described by Khmelinskii et al.50 Briefly, a DNA cassette containing the first 180 bp of the tag, two I-SceI restriction sites surrounding a selectable marker for the synthesis of uracil (URA3) and the full-length tag was inserted into the desired parental strain. Transformed colonies were plated on plates containing galactose to induce the expression of I-SceI. This causes the excision of the URA3 marker and homologous recombination between the N-terminal fragment of the tag and the full-length tag. Finally, colonies are plated onto 5-FOA plates to test for the successful removal of URA3 marker. For all strains, the correct integration of inserts was validated by colony PCR. Moreover, fluorescent tags were also confirmed by live-cell imaging. Cryo-electron tomography Sample preparation and tomogram acquisition To prepare samples for cryo-ET,23 cells expressing exocyst-mNG or mSc3-Sec9 were grown in YPD at 30 °C and 200 rpm overnight. The next morning, they were diluted and grown until they reached OD600 = 0.6, thereafter glycerol was added to a final concentration of 5%. In the case of the Sec18-FRB depletion strain, cells were incubated with 10μM of rapamycin for 10 to 15 minutes. 4 μL of cells were deposited on glow-discharged Cu 200 mesh R1.2/1.3 grids (Quantifoil), 3.5 μL on the front and 0.5 μL at the back side. The grids were blotted and then plunged frozen into liquid ethane by back-side blotting for 4 s using an automated Plunge Freezer EM GP2 (Leica). Grids were clipped in FIB-compatible autogrid cartridges, loaded into an Aquilos 2 Cryo-FIB (ThermoFisher Scientific) and coated with platinum for FIB-SEM milling.22 Lamellae were prepared with AutoTEM (ThermoFisher Scientific) software to a target thickness of 160-180 nm. Automatic rough milling was performed with 3 steps, with 1 nA, 0.5 nA and 0.3 nA respectively. After rough milling on all sites, automatic polishing was performed with 50 pA and 30 pA. Lastly, manual polishing with 30 pA at 0.5⁰ overtilt was performed to further improve the quality of the lamellae. Cryo-fluorescence Z-stack images of lamellae were acquired with 100X objective (0.75 NA) in AiryScan mode on LSM900 (Zeiss) equipped with a cryo-stage (Linkam). 488 nm and 561 nm lasers were used to acquire exocyst-mNG and mSc3-Sec9 images, respectively. The Z-stacks were aligned with StackReg,51 then maximum intensity projection was done in Fiji52 for later correlation. At EMBL Imaging Centre, grids with lamellae were loaded into a Titan Krios G4 (ThermoFisher Scientific) equipped with SelectrisX energy filter and Falcon4i camera, operated with SerialEM software.53 Medium magnification montages of the lamellae were acquired and blended with Etomo.54 Then medium-mag-montages and their corresponding fluorescence map were registered in ICY with ec-CLEMv2 plugin,55 so that the fluorescence signal could be used to guide the high-magnification tilt series collection. Dose-symmetric tilt-series were acquired in SerialEM with PACE-tomo56 during three sessions with different acquisition parameters. The tilts series were recorded over a tilt range of 108° where possible, starting from the milling angle, with an angular increment of 2° or 3°. The total dose of the tilt series was 140e/A2. The raw frames were acquired and stored in EER format, then later processed to reduce beam-induced motion. Tilt-series were acquired with a pixel size between 1.96 and 3.04 Å, with defocus. Table S3 summarizes and compares the acquisition parameters of the four batches. Tilt series processing A total of 736 tilt series were acquired in four batches. In three of these batches, cells with the exocyst fused to mNeonGreen (exocyst-mNG) were used, while the other batch corresponds to cells where Sec9 has been N-terminally tagged with mScarlet3 (mSc3-Sec9). For batch 1 (exocyst-mNG, pixel size = 3.044 Å, 57 tilt images in angular steps of 2° between -46° and 66°) frame alignment for motion correction was performed with the implementation of the UCSF motioncor2 program in Relion 457 using whole frame correction. For batch 2 (exocyst-mNG, pixel size = 1.968 Å, 37 tilt images in angular steps of 3° between -63° and 45°), batch 3 (mSc3-Sec9, pixel size = 1.968 Å, 37 tilt images in angular steps of 3° between -45° and 63°) and batch 4 (exocyst-mNG, pixel size = 1.968 Å, 41 tilt images in angular steps of 3° between -66° and 54°) frame alignment for motion correction was performed in Relion 457 using 25 patches. Tomographic alignment and reconstruction of each tilt series in batches 1 and 4 was performed with AreTomo 1.2.058 and in batches 2 and 3 with IMOD 4.11.1254 using patch-tracking.59 A total of 76, 112, 220 and 328 tilt series were acquired for batch 1, 2, 3 and 4, respectively. All tomograms were reconstructed using either the SART algorithm provided by the Aretomo package58 or the SIRT-like reconstruction protocol of IMOD.54,59 Tomogram annotation and inspection were done in Dynamo.60 All recorded tilt series have been made public in EMPIAR61 under the accession code EMPIAR-12989. Tomogram analysis Segmentation of membranes Membrain-Seg62 was used to identify pixels potentially belonging to membranes using the pre-trained MemBraine_seg_v10_alpha weights on a version of the tomograms downsampled four times. For each tomogram, the normalized score map produced by Membrain-Seg was binarized (with an intensity threshold of 0). The content of the binarized map was analyzed through Matlab's bwconcomp function to reveal the connected components in the tomogram. Connected parts were divided into coherent supervoxels with an in-house, Matlab based code, aiming at identifying coherent regions of a characteristic volume of about 5000 voxels, assumed to be fragments of membranes. Edge filtering of the corresponding regions in the tomogram allowed for assigning to each supervoxel a normal vector that captured the orientation of the membrane fragment it contained. The centroids of those supervoxels were then clustered by DBSCAN in its Matlab implementation. We used an ad-hoc built distance metrics that promotes grouping supervoxels according to local norm similarity and to mutual positioning in an orthogonal arrangement to both normals. In general, this automatic procedure produces very few classification errors: assignment of supervoxels from different membranes to the same cluster is a rare event. Also rare, but more frequent, is the failure to cluster all fragments of the same membrane into the same class: in some cases, the PM of a yeast cell appears not as a single entity but distributed in a few areas. Such cases were identified and manually curated during visual inspection of results. Finally, in order to generate a smooth representation of each membrane, the centroids in a class were used as input for the alphaShape algorithm63 in Matlab with the smallest alpha radius for which all centroids are connected. This results in a triangulation of arbitrary mesh parameters, allowing for a fine sampling of the membrane geometry. Vesicle radius and distance to PM estimation The initial evaluation of vesicle radius and their distribution in relation to the distance to the plasma membrane (Figure 1A) was performed using tomograms from batches 1 and 2. A two-step procedure was applied to improve the quality of the measurements. The first step consisted in a visual inspection of the tomograms with the goal of removing those tomograms that presented global issues such as problematic vitrification, ice contamination, broken lamellas or similar issues that caused deformations during the alignment procedure. The second step consisted in a second round of visual inspection focusing on the quality of the vesicles and the plasma membrane. The reasons for the exclusion of tomograms in this step were: i) vesicles that were too close to the edges of the tomogram, ii) vesicles damaged by the FIB-milling procedure, and iii) unclear definition of membrane boundaries. This two-step analysis reduced the number of tomograms from 188 to 61, allowing the modelling of 370 vesicles and the computation of the radius and vesicle-PM distances using the method described below. Table S4 summarizes the characteristics of the vesicles used for this measurement. Measurement of vesicle-PM distance The simple geometry of vesicles made it possible to identify them by manual picking using a spherical model followed by fast visual curation. This was done using the dtsmlice GUI of Dynamo.60 Dipoles models were manually created on the tomograms. Then, the correspondences between vesicles in the tomogram and models were inspected visually by representing the model as a super-imposed transparent sphere. As such, the vesicles were described merely by their central point and radius. The distance from each vesicle to the closest point in the PM was computed by searching to the closest barycenter in the smooth triangulation provided in the previous step to the vesicle centers. This information was then compensated by the vesicle radius to give an initial automatic estimation of vesicle-PM distance. A further estimation of the vesicle-PM distance was then done manually. In this approach, for each vesicle, the previous estimation of the vesicle-PM geometry was used to define a plane that sectioned the vesicle and crossed the closest point of vesicle and the closest point of the PM. This plane was used to generate and represent an image that was used to manually select more precise estimations of the closest points on the surface of the vesicle and the surface of the plasma membrane. The relative distance between these points was considered an updated estimation of the vesicle-PM distance. This typically resulted in a change of the estimated distances in the order of the nanometer, as the thickness of the membranes can be taken into account more precisely. Selection of isolated vesicles To select isolated vesicles that correlated with exocyst-mNG or mSc3-Sec9 clusters, the following criteria were used: i) a diffraction-limited fluorescence spot had to be observed close to the PM, ii) the vesicle had to be closer than 70 nm from the PM, iii) the vesicle had to be at the center of the tomogram (i.e., >250 nm from the edge), and iv) no vesicles closer than 250 nm could be observed. The estimation of vesicle-PM distance of vesicles correlating with exocyst-mNG signal was performed on the batches 1, 2 and 4. After applying the filtering described above, the number of tomograms was reduced from 516 to 70, allowing the modelling of 76 isolated vesicles. For tomograms in batch 3 (mSc3-Sec9) an additional filtering step was applied: all isolated vesicles were visually inspected to ensure that the closest membrane to the vesicle was the PM. This procedure reduced the number of used tomograms from 220 to 5, allowing the modelling of 5 isolated vesicles. Table S5 summarizes the characteristics of isolated vesicles used for distance estimation. Measurement of vesicle sphericity To assess possible deformations in the shape of the exocytic vesicles due to the presence of forces that might deform vesicles along tethering, we compared their shape at the metastable states MS1-3. Each vesicle subtomogram in states MS1, MS2 and MS3 was annotated manually with the dtmslice tomogram viewing tool in the Dynamo package,60 marking an average of ∼300 points on each vesicle. The cloud of points annotated on each vesicle was fitted into an ellipsoid through a Matlab script, assigning to each vesicle a set of directions and lengths that define the orientation and semiaxes of the fitted ellipsoid. Because of the missing wedge in tomographic reconstruction, an elongation in the direction close to the electron beam was systematically detected (Figure S6A). Correlations between the two minor axes of each fitted ellipsoid and the metastable state where the vesicle was found in were analyzed with an in-house Matlab script that was not able to detect relevant deviations from sphericity (Figure S6B). Possible correlations of these parameters and membership in the predefined classes were investigated through in-house Matlab scripts. These results agree with a fast fusion event, but do not rule out the existence of forces that might deform the vesicle shape during the short lapse of time that separates the end of MS3 and the estimated fusion. These measurements were done on isolated vesicles that correlated with exocyst-mNG (40 vesicles) or mSc3-Sec9 signal (5 vesicles). Subtomogram Averaging Several approaches were used for subtomogram averaging (STA) experiments. In a first approach we used Dynamo60 for the alignment of the interstitial space of 281 vesicles extracted from 277 tomograms, from the Batches 2, 3 and 4. Those tomograms were processed using the same protocol SART reconstruction with a common pixel size to allow for a fair comparison between all the particles. From these reconstructions, the distance between vesicles and plasma membrane was measured to classify vesicles into their respective metastable states. To increase the number of particles available for STA, all well-reconstructed particles located sufficiently close to the membrane were included, even if the vesicles were not isolated vesicles. We used the vesicles by selecting as center of the extracted subtomograms the approximate found midpoint between vesicle and plasma membrane. Additionally, the vector defining the closest direction between vesicle and plasma membrane was used as initial orientation of the subtomograms for STA. Such experiments used a pixel size of 7.92 Å and 12.18 Å, and an initial lowpass of at least 16 nm and 24 nm, respectively. They were repeated for different parameter combinations such as field of view of the subtomogram box (ranging between 120 and 240 nm), extent and shape of the mask to selectively exclude areas of the membrane and/or vesicle, and selection of subsets of particles with a homogeneous interstitial distance (MS1, MS2 and MS3 in the text). In a second approach, STA was carried towards the alignment of individual exocyst proteins. In order to possibly limit the number of conformations, we selected the 98 vesicles corresponding to the MS2 state with a pixel size of 7.92 Å, and analyzed the interstitial space with template matching64 searching for individual copies of the exocyst using as template a single particle map of the exocyst complex available in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank65 (accession code: EMD-6827) rescaled to a pixel size of 7.92 Å. The search was performed with an angular interval of 5 degrees. Only the peaks located in the interstitial space were selected for the evaluation in order to avoid false positives originated by the plasma membrane or the vesicle. After extraction of a total of 1394 and 2601 particles for a cross-correlation threshold of 0.2 and an angular coherence of 5 and 20 degrees between the normal of the vesicle and the orientation obtained from template matching, respectively. Several STA experiments were performed, varying the initial orientation of the particles for avoiding the template bias (from an azimuthal randomization to a complete perturbation). Such experiments used an initial lowpass of above 10 nm to avoid transmission of template bias into STA computations. Z-stacks of 21 frames separated by 250 nm were acquired using a 100 ms exposure, utilizing microscope setup 1 (see microscope setups section). The average copy number of the reference, Cse4, has been recently quantified by Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM).25 Cse4 clusters in cells undergoing anaphase were tracked over the Z-stack using TrackMate67 with a spot diameter of 7 pixels. The plane with the highest corrected total intensity (CTI) was determined by 𝐶 𝑇 𝐼 = 𝐼 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 − 𝐼 𝐵 𝐺 ∗ ( 𝐴 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 / 𝐴 𝐵 𝐺 ) , where 𝐼 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 / 𝐵 𝐺 and 𝐴 𝑠 𝑝 𝑜 𝑡 / 𝐵 𝐺 represent the integrated intensity and area of the selected spot and the local background, respectively. The local background is defined as the circular region with twice the diameter of the selected spot and that surrounds this spot. If CTI maximum occurred in the first or last frame, the Cse4 cluster was discarded. Afterwards, PM-associated, isolated and static target protein clusters (fluorescent spots without apparent in-plane movement) were manually chosen. Those events were tracked with a spot-diameter of 3 pixels, and the CTI was calculated as explained before. The target protein copy number ( 𝑛 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 ) was calculated by the stoichiometry ratio 𝑛 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 = 𝑛 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 ∗ ( 𝐼 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 / 𝐼 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 ) , where 𝑛 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 is the number of Cse4 in a cluster (4.8 ± 2.4 Cse4 per kinetochore,25 which leads to 𝑛 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 = 76.8 ± 9.8 Cse4 per cluster during telophase or anaphase), and 𝐼 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 and 𝐼 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 are the median of the CTI values for the corresponding protein target and Cse4, respectively. The error associated to 𝑛 𝑡 𝑎 𝑟 was calculated as described in Picco et al. (2015).24 The average exocyst copy number was obtained by averaging the copy number of all exocyst subunits. Single particle tracking Images were acquired using the microscope setup 2 (see microscope setups section). A cage incubator mounted on the microscope (Okolab) was used to keep a constant 25 °C environment. Simultaneous acquisition was performed with an OptoSplit II Bypass image splitter (Cairn Research). A quadrant of 512x700 pixels centered in the illumination maxima of the camera sensor was used. Movies were acquired at 8.7 frames per second (fps) to a total length of 70 seconds. An exposure time of 80 ms was used, and laser power was manually optimized for each protein. Zyla camera was set to 540 mHz and binning 2. For Sec18 anchor-away (Figure 5B), movies were acquired after a 10 minute 10 μM rapamycin treatment at 2 fps during 2.5 min. Despite slower frame rate and longer movies (required to capture long-lived clusters) the average lifetime of sequestered protein clusters is underestimated because of the technical limitations in detecting long-lived events. Raw movies were preprocessed to remove extracellular background using the rolling ball algorithm in Fiji,52 with a ball radius of 60 pixels. Afterwards, the images were bleach-corrected by the Exponential Fitting plugin in Fiji.68 Finally, a 3D Gaussian-filter with radius 0.5 pixels in X and Y axes and 2 pixels in time axis was applied to Exo84-mCh channel (hereafter channel 1 or C1). C1 spots were tracked with TrackMate,67 setting the Difference of Gaussians (DoG) method with a particle diameter of 3 pixels. Simple LAP tracker was set with a linking maximum distance of 1.5 pixels and a distance and frame gap of 2 pixels and 1 frame respectively. Tracks closer than 10 pixels from the image borders and those with a duration shorter than 10 frames were discarded. The polarized nature of exocytosis challenges the detection of isolated events. To aid the detection of isolated exocytotic events we included three additional features into TrackMate: Track_Quality_Enviroment, Track_Quality_Before and Track_Quality_After. All three are computed over the 32-bits DoG-filtered movie. Track_Quality_Enviroment is defined as the mean intensity of the local background along the track (i.e., pixels at 2 and 3 pixels from the mean track centroid). A value close to zero of this feature indicates a uniform background signal along the track duration (i.e., no track overlapping has occurred). Track_Quality_Before and Track_Quality_After are the mean intensity of those pixels within a distance of 1.5 pixels from the mean track centroid ∼500 ms before the track start and ∼500 ms after the track end, respectively. High values of these features might indicate overlapping with neighboring tracks or a deficient tracking, since the intensity at the exocytic site is expected to be close to background levels just before and after exocyst clustering. Integrating these three features with those computed by TrackMate resulted in a list of filtered tracks, where the clustering and release of the exocyst is clearly identified. Tracks were then manually curated. For those manually curated C1-tracks, we inspected the second channel in the same location of the respective C1-track to look for the presence of a diffraction-limited spot of the corresponding mNG-tagged protein (hereafter channel 2 or C2). If unambiguously colocalized in space with the C1-track, they were tracked using TrackMate with ad-hoc adjustments to optimize the C2 spot-detection and linking. Once C2 tracking was completed, clustering and release times were computed with respect to the last detected frame in C1 (TRACK_STOP feature), i.e., C2-clustering time = (TRACK_START_C2 - TRACK_STOP_C1) and C2-release time = (TRACK_STOP_C2 - TRACK_STOP_C1). In the specific case of Sec18-mNG, the corrected intensity profiles for C1 and C2, defined as (Mean_Spot_Intensity - Mean_local_Background_Intensity), were extracted from the raw images; where Mean_Spot_Intensity is the mean of intensities of pixels within 1.5 pixels from the spot centroid, and Mean_local_Background_Intensity is the mean of intensities of pixels located at 2 and 3 pixels from the spot centroid. The profiles of Exo84-mCh and Sec18-mNG were aligned to the TRACK_STOP_C1 frame, normalized to their corresponding maximum value and then averaged. In the case of tracking mNG-Sec1 with Sec18 depletion (Figure S6D), images were also acquired with microscope setup 2, but only with a single channel (488 nm) on which single particle tracking was performed. In the case of Exo84-mNG cluster initiation analysis (Figure 5F), images were acquired using microscope setup 1 (see microscope setups section), at 1 frame per second, before and after Sec18-FRB depletion (15 minutes of 10 μM rapamycin treatment). Single particle tracking of one channel was performed as outlined above, except for Track_Quality_After filter, which was not utilized. Thus, only the initiation of tracks had to pass quality control. After manual curation of Exo84-mCh initiated tracks, the count of curated tracks was divided by the total number of cells. Sec18 anchor-away recruitment This approach is based on the sequestration of a protein tagged to the FKBP-rapamycin binding (FRB) domain by a rapamycin-based inducible translocation to an anchoring platform labeled with the FK506-binding protein (FKBP) by a rapamicyn-induced translocation.32 To induce the depletion of Sec18 from exocytic sites, we fused FKBP to the C-terminus of Pil1 (Pil1-FKBP), a BAR domain containing protein that is a core component of eisosomes.70 To be able to visualize the anchors, we labeled them with an RFP tag (Pil1-FKBP-RFP). We fused the FRB domain and GFP to the C-terminus of Sec18 (Sec18-FRB-GFP). FKBP and FRB tags heterodimerize in the presence of the small molecule rapamycin.32,71 Cells were attached to Concanavalin A-coated coverslips and rapamycin was added to a final concentration of 10 μM. To select the optimal rapamycin incubation time and minimize the likelihood of undesired secondary functional impairments, we analyzed the time course of the Sec18-FRB-GFP sequestration (Figure S5D). Wide-field fluorescent microscopy images were obtained using microscope setup 3 (see microscope setups section). Red- and green-channel images were sequentially acquired every 5 min. Exposure times were 200 ms and 1000 ms for red and green channels, respectively. The workflow for analyzing colocalization between the anchor and the target protein was implemented as an ImageJ macro which essentially calculated the area of overlap between spots independently segmented in images from the red (anchor) and green (target) channels. A more detailed explanation of this macro is described in Pazos et al. (2023).72 By weighting the overlapping area by the total area of the green-labeled protein we obtained a colocalization score that is indicative of the amount of Sec18-FRB-GFP translocated at the anchoring platforms. Upon 5 minutes of treatment, the sequestration of Sec18-FRB-GFP reached saturation (Figure S5D). As shown by fluorescence microscopy (Figure S5B), a significant fraction of the AAA ATPase remained free after rapamycin treatment. Up to 20 minutes of treatment, we could not detect any decrease in the flow of secretory vesicles that are transported from the mother cell to the bud and in the number of secretory vesicles that accumulate near the PM (Figures S5E and S5F), ruling out possible defects upstream of exocytosis. Thereafter, we treated cells with rapamycin between 10 and 15 minutes to specifically investigate the role of Sec18 in the dynamics of the ExHOS. Vesicle transport assay using FRAP Images were acquired using the microscope setup 4 (see microscope setups section), at 8.7 fps to a total length of 35 seconds. Two initial frames were taken using the TIRF 488 nm laser, followed by photobleaching of yeast cell buds for 2 frames using the 488 nm FRAP laser, followed by 300 frames during photobleaching recovery. 488 nm TIRF laser was used with an exposure time of 80 ms, and 488 nm FRAP laser an exposure time of 116 ms (with 2 repetitions). Zyla camera was set to 540 mHz and binning 2. For Sec18 anchor-away, movies were acquired after 10-20 minutes of 10 μM rapamycin treatment. To analyze Sec2-posiitve vesicle transport into buds, bleached bud necks were monitored across the movies and positively counted when a diffraction limited Sec2 cluster passed from mother into bud cell across this interface. PICT assay The Protein interactions from Imaging Complexes after Translocation (PICT) technique33 enables the quantitative characterization of protein interactions in vivo. The addition of rapamycin to the culture medium induces FRB-FKBP heterodimerization, leading to the translocation of the FRB-tagged bait protein (bait-FRB) to anchoring platforms engineered in the cell. These platforms are generated by tagging an anchoring molecule with mCh and FKBP (anchor-mCh-FKBP). Prey proteins tagged with mNG (prey-mNG) that interact with bait-FRB are co-translocated to these anchoring platforms. These localization changes can then be quantified using dual-colour live-cell imaging. All PICT experiments were performed in rapamycin-insensitive yeast strains carrying the tor1-1 mutation in the TOR1 gene and a deletion of the FPR1 gene.33 Images were acquired before and after rapamycin addition. For the PICT assay, yeast strains expressing the Sla2-mCh-FKBP anchor and harboring Sec15-FRB (bait) and Sec18-mNG (prey) were used. When required, 10 μM rapamycin was added 20 minutes before imaging, and 200 μM latrunculin A (Lat A) was added 10 minutes before imaging, ensuring Lat A treatment did not exceed 10 minutes. Imaging was performed using microscope setup 5. Red and green channels were acquired sequentially, and fluorescent TetraSpeck microspheres (0.1 μm, blue/green/orange/dark red) were used to correct chromatic aberration. A custom image analysis workflow was implemented as a Fiji macro to automate data processing. This workflow estimated co-localization between independently segmented mCh (anchor) and mNG (prey) spots. The recruitment score was determined by measuring the area of overlap between the mNG and mCh channels, quantified by counting the number of foreground pixels common to both segmentation masks (logical AND operation) across all fields of view. For analysis, the recruitment score was estimated in cells under No rapamycin (- rap) and +Rapamycin (+ rap) conditions.
