Bgl2 secretion assay Bgl2 secretion assays were performed as previously described73 with minor modifications. Briefly, a FRB-absent control strain and a strain expressing Sec18-FRB were grown overnight at 30°C and 200 rpm until saturation. Cultures were diluted in 20 mL YPD and grown at 30°C to an OD600 of 1. Sodium azide (NaN3) and Sodium fluoride (NaF) were added to a final concentration of 10 mM each. Cells were pelleted by centrifugation (2500 rpm, room temperature, 5 min), washed twice in 20 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 10 mM NaN3, 10 mM NaF, and resuspended in 300 μL of spheroplast solution buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 1.4 M sorbitol, 10 mM NaN3, 10 mM NaF, 30 mM2-Mercaptoethanol, 0.2 mg/mL zymolyase. Spheroplast formation was carried out at 37°C for 30 minutes. The spheroplasts were centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 minutes at 4°C, and 100 μL of the supernatant was mixed with 20 μL of 6x SDS sample buffer. The remaining supernatant was removed, and spheroplasts were washed twice in spheroplast washing buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 1.4 M D-Sorbitol, 10 mM NaN3, 10 mM NaF). For intracellular protein extraction, spheroplasts were lysed in 20 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 2 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 1x protease inhibitor cocktail (100 ng/mL of Antipain, Leupeptin, Pepstatin A, in DMSO and 1mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride PMSF) and incubated on ice for 10 minutes. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation at 13000 rpm for 5 minutes at 4°C, and 100 μL of the supernatant was mixed with 20 μL of 6x SDS sample buffer. Samples were denatured at 95°C for 5 minutes and analyzed by SDS-PAGE and Western blot using an anti-Bgl2 antibody (gift from Prof. Randy Schekman, 1:2,000 dilution in TBST + 5% milk). Three replica blots were analyzed. Band intensities were quantified using Fiji Gel Analyzer52 and normalized to total protein levels (Ponceau S staining). Calculation of % secretion of Bgl2: External intensity/(External intensity + Internal intensity) x 100. Spot assay of yeast growth An initial cell suspension at OD₆₀₀ = 1 was prepared, followed by 1:10 serial dilutions. Cells were then spotted onto YPD plates containing 10 μM rapamycin and incubated for 24 hours. Affinity purification-mass spectrometry Affinity purification with crosslinking Yeast cells were grown overnight at 30°C and 180 rpm until saturation. Cultures were diluted in 600 mL YPD and grown at 30°C to an OD600 of 0.8-1. Cells were harvested by centrifugation (1000 x g, 10 min, 4°C), and washed twice with resuspension buffer (50 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.4 supplemented with protease inhibitors (100 ng/mL of Antipain, Leupeptin and Pepstatin A in DMSO and 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride PMSF). The final pellet was resuspended in 1 mL resuspension buffer and quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen in a drop-by-drop fashion. Cell lysis was performed using Freezer/Mill® model 6775 (1 min pre-cooling, 2 min running, 1 min interval, 1 min cooling, rate: 11, cycles: 3) (SPEX SamplePrep, LLC). Lysates were resuspended in 5 mL resuspension buffer and clarified by centrifugation at 17,000 × g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected for downstream processing. A fresh stock solution of disuccinimidyl suberate (DSS) (100 mM), a cross-linker 11.4 Å in length, was equilibrated at room temperature for 10 min before use. Cross-linking was initiated by adding DSS to the lysate at a final concentration of 0.5 mM, followed by incubation at room temperature for 1 hour with gentle mixing. The reaction was quenched by adding glycine to a final concentration of 100 mM and incubating for 15 min at room temperature. Samples were centrifuged (17,000 × g, 10 min, 4°C), and the clarified supernatant was used for immunoprecipitation. GFP-Trap and blocking agarose beads were equilibrated by washing five times in PBS. For each sample, 90μL of blocking beads were incubated with the lysate for 1 hour at 4°C on an orbital shaker to reduce nonspecific binding. The blocked lysate was collected by centrifugation (7000 rpm, 30 sec, 4°C) and transferred to fresh tubes containing 90μL of GFP-Trap beads. Samples were incubated overnight at 4°C on an orbital shaker. The next day, beads were collected by centrifugation, washed five times with a stringent buffer (2M NaCl, 8M urea, 1% Triton X-100) and five times with PBS, changing tubes after the last wash in each condition. Mass spectrometry Beads used in immunoprecipitation were cleaned three times with 500 μl of 200 mM ammonium bicarbonate and 60 μl of 6M Urea/200mM ammonium bicarbonate were added. Samples were then reduced with dithiothreitol (30 nmol, 37 °C, 60 min), alkylated in the dark with iodoacetamide (60 nmol, 25 °C, 30 min) and diluted to 1M urea with 200 mM ammonium bicarbonate for trypsin digestion (1 μg, 37°C, 8h). After digestion, peptide mix was acidified with formic acid and desalted with a MicroSpin C18 column prior to LC-MS/MS analysis. Samples were analyzed using a Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific) coupled to an EASY-nLC 1200 (ThermoFisher Scientific). Peptides were loaded directly onto the analytical column and were separated by reversed-phase chromatography using a 50-cm column with an inner diameter of 75 μm, packed with 2 μm C18 particles. Chromatographic gradients started at 95% buffer A and 5% buffer B with a flow rate of 300 nl/min and gradually increased to 25% buffer B and 75% A in 52 min and then to 40% buffer B and 60% A in 8 min. After each analysis, the column was washed for 10 min with 100% buffer B. Buffer A: 0.1% formic acid in water. Buffer B: 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The mass spectrometer was operated in positive ionization mode with nanospray voltage set at 2.4 kV and source temperature at 305°C. The acquisition was performed in data-dependent adquisition (DDA) mode and full MS scans with 1 micro scans at resolution of 120000 were used over a mass range of m/z 350-1400 with detection in the Orbitrap mass analyzer. Auto gain control (AGC) was set to ‘standard’ and injection time to ‘auto’. In each cycle of data-dependent acquisition analysis, following each survey scan, the most intense ions above a threshold ion count of 10000 were selected for fragmentation. The number of selected precursor ions for fragmentation was determined by the “Top Speed” acquisition algorithm and a dynamic exclusion of 60 seconds. Fragment ion spectra were produced via high-energy collision dissociation (HCD) at normalized collision energy of 28% and they were acquired in the ion trap mass analyzer. AGC and injection time were set to ‘Standard’ and ‘Dynamic’, respectively and isolation window of 1.4 m/z was used. Digested bovine serum albumin was analyzed between each sample to avoid sample carryover and to assure stability of the instrument and QCloud74 has been used to control instrument longitudinal performance during the project. Acquired spectra were analysed using the Proteome Discoverer software suite (v2.5) and the Mascot search engine (v2.6).75 The data were searches against a Saccharomyces Genome database (as in April 2022, 6049 entries) plus a list76 of common contaminants and all the corresponding decoy entries. For peptide identification, a precursor ion mass tolerance of 7 ppm was used for MS1 level, trypsin was chosen as enzyme and up to three missed cleavages were allowed. The fragment ion mass tolerance was set to 0.5 Da for MS2 spectra. Oxidation of methionine and N-terminal protein acetylation were used as variable modifications whereas carbamidomethylation on cysteines was set as a fixed modification. False discovery rate (FDR) in peptide identification was set to a maximum of 1%. Peptide quantification data were retrieved from the “Precursor ions quantifier” node from Proteome Discoverer (v2.5) using 2 ppm mass tolerance for the peptide extracted ion current (XIC). The obtained values were normalized with the median of EXO84 and have used to calculate protein fold-changes and their corresponding p-value and adjusted p-values. The raw proteomics data have been deposited to the PRIDE77 repository with the dataset identifier PXD061766. Single Molecule Localization Microscopy Sample preparation for SMLM Sample preparation for SMLM26 was performed as previously described.78 Briefly, yeast cells were grown at 30 °C and 180 rpm overnight until saturation. The next morning, the cultures were diluted and grown at 30°C to an OD600 = 0.8. 2 ml of culture was pelleted (2500 rpm), resuspended in 100 μl of YPD and pipetted onto a Concanavalin A-coated coverslip. After 15 minutes in a humidified atmosphere, the non-attached cells were removed by decantation. For the Sec18 anchor-away, after 5 minutes of attachment, rapamycin was added to a final concentration of 10 μM and incubated for 10 more minutes. Coverslips were then submerged into a freshly prepared fixation solution (4% paraformaldehyde and 2% sucrose in PBS). After 15 minutes of gentle shaking, they were removed from the fixation solution and submerged into a quenching solution (100 mM NH4Cl in PBS) for 15 minutes with gentle shaking. Quenching was repeated twice. Finally, coverslips were washed three times in PBS for 5 min. SMLM imaging All Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) images were acquired on a custom-built, fully automated microscope, which was built for stable long-term automated image acquisition, and featured homogeneous high-power illumination as described previously.79 The free-space output of a commercial LightHUB laser box with 405 nm, 488 nm, 561 nm and 638 nm laser lines was focused on a speckle reducer and coupled into a multimode fiber. The output of the fiber was then imaged into the sample to homogenously illuminate a circular area of ∼1000 mm. Fluorescence was collected through a 160x NA 1.43 TIRF objective (Leica), filtered by a bandpass filter (for GFP: 525/50; for mMaple: 600/60), and focused onto an Evolve512D EMCCD camera. The z focus was optically stabilized by total internally reflecting an additional IR laser off the coverslip onto a quadrant photo diode, which was coupled into an electronic feedback loop with the piezo objective positioner. Z focus stability was typically better than 5 nm/h. All microscope components are controlled by a custom-written plugin for μManager.80 Samples were mounted in 1 mL of imaging buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8 in 95% D2O) and sealed with parafilm to prevent evaporation. The back focal plane was imaged and visually inspected to make sure no air bubbles were present in the immersion oil. Then, videos of 15000-50000 frames were acquired using the 561 nm laser at 7-9 kW/cm2 with an exposure time of 30 ms, and a camera EM gain and readout rate of 200 and 10 MHz, respectively. During acquisition, mMaple was slowly photoconverted to its red state by 405 nm illumination. The 405 nm pulse duration was controlled through an automatic feedback loop to maintain the number of blinks constant. When all mMaple was photoconverted and no more blinking was observed, acquisition was stopped. Photoconversion parameters were optimized so that no overlapping point spread functions (PSFs) were observed. After acquiring SMLM data, a diffraction-limited snapshot of GFP or mNG signal was collected using a 488 nm laser and the same camera parameters as previously described. To automatically image multiple regions of one sample, the stage position list of μManager was used to define a grid of 80-100 positions. There was a separation of 200 μm in each X and Y direction between positions to avoid undesired photoactivation and photobleaching due to scattered light. A waiting time of 3 s was established between positions to allow for mechanical equilibration of the stage after its movement. SMLM data processing and analysis Super-resolution microscopy analysis platform (SMAP) was used to reconstruct SMLM data.81 All images were automatically fitted during acquisition. For the reconstruction, all localizations found in consecutive frames within a range of 75 nm were grouped into one localization. Localizations with a PSF standard deviation greater than 160 nm and a localization precision that exceeded 25 nm were discarded. To visualize the images, localizations were rendered using Gaussian kernels with a standard deviation proportional to their localization precision. A minimum Gaussian standard deviation of 6 nm was used. To correct for chromatic aberrations between SMLM and diffraction-limited (DL) images, a predetermined transformation was used to align red (photoconverted mMaple) and green (GFP or mNG) images. The transformation was created by imaging and localizing more than 1000 TetraSpeck beads in both channels. Then, a projective transformation was created from their positions. This correction was also done using SMAP. To select isolated exocytic sites, cells were first automatically segmented by the “SegmentCellsCME” plugin from SMAP. Each cell was visualized using SMAP ROI manager, from where individual clusters (correlating to isolated DL GFP or mNG spots) were identified. Exocyst clusters were only segmented at the center of the cell surface to avoid tilted structures. Those DL spots that were not in the central region of the cell surface or that did not colocalize with mMaple signal were manually discarded. Finally, just those selected sites containing more than 30 localizations –which correspond to 3 exocysts on average- were considered for further analysis. SMLM copy number quantification Nuclear pore complex (NPC) proteins can be used as reference standards for assessing molecular counting in SMLM experiments.28 Following this idea, yeast cells expressing Nup188, an NPC subunit, labeled with mMaple (Nup188-mM), were imaged using the optical settings previously described. The segmentation of Nup188-mM clusters was done manually using the ROI Manager interface of SMAP. The mean ( 𝐿 𝑅 ) and standard deviation ( 𝜎 𝑅 ) of the distribution of localizations per Nup188-mM cluster was used to estimate the number of exocysts ( 𝑁 𝑇 ) , by computing the ratio 𝑁 𝑇 = ( 𝐿 𝑇 / 𝐿 𝑅 ) ∗ 𝑁 𝑅 / 3 , where 𝐿 𝑇 is the mean number localizations per exocyst-mM or exocyst-mM-GFP cluster, 𝑁 𝑅 = 16 is the average number of Nup188 per NPC28 and the factor 3 accounts for each exocyst being labeled with 3 mMaples. The error associated with 𝑁 𝑇 is calculated as 𝑁 𝑇 ∗ ( 𝜎 𝑅 / 𝐿 𝑅 ) 2 + ( 𝜎 𝑇 / 𝐿 𝑇 ) 2 . All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. SMLM analysis Modeling the conformational space of ExHOS We aimed to model the space of possible higher-order structures in which multiple exocysts can bind the vesicle and the PM simultaneously. To do this, the exocyst was represented as a rigid cylinder with a height ( 𝐿 𝑒 ) of 32 nm and a diameter ( 𝑊 𝑒 ) of 13 nm, based on the overall exocyst dimensions in the cryo-EM structure (PDB82: 5YFP). Note that this is likely an underestimation of the exocyst dimensions as 18% of the exocyst amino acids, mostly Sec3 and Exo84 N-termini, could not be resolved. The vesicle was represented as a sphere of radius ( 𝑟 𝑣 ) of 41.2 nm (this value was derived from the cryo-ET experiments, see Figure 1). Additionally, the effective radius ( 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 𝑓 ) of the vesicle was increased by 4 nm to account for the minimal space that the Sec4-Sec2 complex occupies on the vesicle surface (PDB: 2OCY). Assuming (i) the exocyst-vesicle and exocyst-PM binding sites are located at the extreme of the axial axis of the cylinder and (ii) the exocysts are bound radially outwards to the vesicle, the allowed configurations can be parametrized with an angle 𝜃 varying in the range [ 0 , 𝜋 / 2 ] , where 𝜃 = 0 when the longest axis of the exocysts are orthogonal to the PM, and 𝜃 = 𝜋 / 2 when the longest axis of the exocysts are parallel to the PM. For a given exocyst, we defined the coordinates of the contact point with the PM { 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 𝑧 0 } and the coordinates of the contact point with Sec4-Sec2 complex at the vesicle surface { 𝑥 1 , 𝑦 1 , 𝑧 1 } as follows: { 𝑥 0 , 𝑦 0 , 𝑧 0 } = { 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 𝑓 cos 𝜃 , 0 , 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 + 𝑟 𝑣 − 𝑟 𝑒 𝑓 𝑓 sin 𝜃 } { 𝑥 1 , 𝑦 1 , 𝑧 1 } = { 𝑥 0 ± 𝐿 𝑒 2 − 𝑧 0 2 , 0 , 0 } , where 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 is the vesicle-PM distance. We were particularly interested in the radial position (respect to the shortest axis between the vesicle and the PM) of the exocyst centroids (ρ), that can be computed as ( 𝑥 0 + 𝑥 1 ) / 2 . This parameter served us as descriptor of the ExHOS. The underlying organization of the ExHOS highly depends on the conformational relationship among the exocysts present. For example, a heterogeneous ExHOS where the multiple exocysts are positioned in random locations, but always fulfilling the condition of binding the vesicle and the PM simultaneously. On the other hand, a homotypic ExHOS where the exocysts adopt the same conformation relative to the vesicle and the PM leads to ring-shaped ExHOSs (all ρ’s values would be equal). In this case, the maximum number of exocysts ( 𝑁 max ) can be approximated as 𝑁 max = 𝑥 0 / 𝑊 𝑒 and the coordinates for jth exocyst can be obtained by applying a rotation with angle 2 𝜋 / 𝑁 max ∗ 𝑗 around the Z-axis. In the homotypic situation, the radius of the resulting ring-shaped ExHOS depends on the 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 and 𝑁 𝑚 𝑎 𝑥 . By imposing 𝑁 max ≥ 6 (since the average number of exocysts determined by live-cell imaging was 7 ± 1 exocysts in each cluster; Figures 1B and S1D), the distal tethering ( 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 = 31 nm) leads to exocyst configurations of radius within 15-22 nm. Instead, for the proximal tethering ( 𝑑 𝑉 − 𝑃 𝑀 = 4 nm ), radii in the range 28-50 nm are possible (Figure 1D). All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. Synthetic SMLM datasets We simulated a set of SMLM images for all the possible higher-order structures modeled for distal and proximal tethering. Firstly, between 6 and 8 exocyst centroids were distributed uniformly along a ring (or randomly inside a patch) of radius 𝑟 for a homotypic (or the heterotypic) ExHOS. For each exocyst, three mMaple were positioned randomly, with their centroids following a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution with zero mean and a standard deviation of 10 nm along each direction. Each mMaple had a probability of emitting of 0.55, as previously determined.28 The number of blinking events, 𝑛 , per emitting mMaple was simulated using a log-normal distribution with parameters obtained from the fit of the number of localizations per cluster of the Nup188-mM (Figure S2). Finally, the localizations were distributed around each mMaple centroid position following a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution with zero mean and a standard deviation corresponding to an average localization precision of 20 nm along each direction. The resulting set of XY-coordinates from the generated localizations was used for image rendering and subsequent analysis. For Compact and Expanded ExHOS, synthetic images were randomly selected from 𝑟 values in the range from 15 to 22 nm and from 28 to 50 nm, respectively. All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. SMLM data classification For a given synthetic SMLM image containing the set of N localizations with coordinates { 𝑥 𝑗 , 𝑦 𝑗 } , with j=1,···,N, a ring center { 𝑐 𝑥 , 𝑐 𝑦 } and radius 𝑅 𝑇 estimated using the Taubin algorithm83 implemented in the Python library circle_fit that aims to minimize the algebraic function 𝐹 ( 𝑐 𝑥 , 𝑐 𝑦 , 𝑅 𝑇 ) = ∑ 𝑗 = 1 𝑁 [ ( 𝑥 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑥 ) 2 + ( 𝑦 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑥 ) 2 − 𝑅 𝑇 2 ] 2 / ∑ 𝑗 = 1 𝑁 [ ( 𝑥 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑥 ) 2 + ( 𝑦 𝑗 − 𝑐 𝑦 ) 2 ] 2 Taubin’s center estimation achieves the lower Kanati-Cramer-Rao bound,84 which establishes a limit of the precision of the parameter estimation given the average SMLM resolution. In addition to 𝑅 𝑇 and its associated error, a series of geometrical features were computed for all the synthetic images based on the Taubin center, including the first and second circular moment and the inner radius. The gyration radius, which does not rely on the Taubin center, was also considered. The mathematical expressions for all these geometrical features are provided in Figure S4. A matrix containing the values of the geometrical features for all the synthetic images was generated. This matrix served as input for training a random forest classifier to classify the synthetic SMLM images into the categories Compact and Expanded ExHOS, implemented using the ensemble.RandomForestClassifier library from Scikit Learn 1.3.2.85 We performed a randomized grid search to tune the model's hyperparameters. The optimal configuration utilized 100 decision trees, a maximum tree depth of 5, and considered the square root of the total features at each split (max_features=”sqrt”), with bootstrap sampling. This model achieved an average accuracy of 0.90 in classifying the synthetic data. The relative importance of the geometrical features in the random forest model and the average images of the predicted classes are shown in Figure S4. Finally, after computing the described geometrical features for the experimental set of images of isolated exocyst-mM (or exocyst-mM-GFP) clusters, the optimized random forest classifier was applied to predict the ExHOS class (Compact or Expanded). This prediction was repeated 30 times with randomizations of the training dataset, and the average prediction result was reported (Figure S4A). All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. SMLM averaging and ExHOS radius estimation Those images belonging to a class (Compact or Expanded) were aligned to their Taubin’s center and weighted-averaged, i.e., 𝐼 𝑎 𝑣 𝑔 ( 𝑥 , 𝑦 ) = ∑ 𝑖 𝜔 𝑖 𝐼 𝑖 ( 𝑥 , 𝑦 ) / ∑ 𝑖 𝜔 𝑖 , where 𝜔 𝑖 is the random forest-score for the i-th image. Then, from the average radial density 𝑔 ( 𝑟 ) , the mean distance-to-center was computed: ∫ 0 ∞ 𝑟 ∗ 𝑔 ( 𝑟 ) 𝑑 𝑟 . Because of the existence of estimation bias of the underlying ExHOS radius,84 a bias-correction was implemented by creating a calibration curve between the underlying radii of the ExHOS and the corresponding localizations mean distance-to-center in the synthetic dataset. Note that, as SMLM localizes tags, potential few-nm systematic offsets may remain despite calibration. All code is available at https://github.com/GallegoLab. Estimation of ExHOS conformational dynamics The transition from Compact to Expanded classes of ExHOS was modeled as a first-order reaction process, according to an effective rate 𝑘 . The relative population of the Compact ExHOS at a given time t after exocyst clustering, 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) , is governed by the differential equation: 𝑑 𝑑 𝑡 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) = 𝑘 ∗ 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) , with 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) + 𝑝 𝐸 𝑥 𝑝 𝑎 𝑛 𝑑 𝑒 𝑑 ( 𝑡 ) = 1 . Based on the trend observed in the Sec2-GFP and mNG-Sec9 correlative SMLM experiments (Figure 4A), it is reasonable to assume that exocysts are organized exclusively in a Compact structure during the initial time-point of the tethering, leading to the condition 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 0 ) = 1 . Therefore, the solution for 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 is given by 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 = exp ( − 𝑘 ∗ 𝑡 ) (Equation 1). The rate constant 𝑘 can be estimated by solving the equation 1 𝑡 𝑓 − 𝑡 0 ∫ 𝑡 0 𝑡 𝑓 𝑝 𝐶 𝑜 𝑚 𝑝 𝑎 𝑐 𝑡 ( 𝑡 ) 𝑑 𝑡 = 𝜌 , where 𝑡 0 and 𝑡 𝑓 are the initial and final time of the given time-window, respectively, and 𝜌 is the frequency of Compact ExHOS experimentally observed within this time frame. The reported errors of 𝑘 and predicted frequency of ExHOS classes were calculated using an error-propagation scheme based on the previous equation. Estimation of the vesicle kinetics Assuming the images obtained by cryo-CLEM provide a uniform sampling of the exocytic event lifetime and that the likelihood that multiple exocysts cluster before the arrival of the vesicle is negligible (which is supported by the enrichment of tomograms without vesicle or PM deformation in the cryo-CLEM of cells expressing mSc3-Sec9), it is reasonable to estimate the fusion time based on the frequency of exocyst-mNG correlated-tomograms with and without vesicles. Then, the likelihood to find a tomogram without a vesicle can be modeled with a binomial distribution with a successful probability pfusion. The error associated to the fraction of no-vesicles tomogram is given by 𝑛 ∗ 𝑝 𝑓 𝑢 𝑠 𝑖 𝑜 𝑛 ∗ ( 1 − 𝑝 𝑓 𝑢 𝑠 𝑖 𝑜 𝑛 ) / 𝑛 , where n is the number of sampled tomograms. Considering n = 95, 𝑝 𝑓 𝑢 𝑠 𝑖 𝑜 𝑛 = 0.2 (from the 19/95 observed no-vesicles tomograms; Figure 6A), and the exocyst cluster lifetime is 9.4 s on average, we estimated vesicle fusion occur 1.9 ± 0.4 s before exocyst release (or similarly, 7.5 ± 0.4 s after exocyst clustering), on average. The related error can be estimated by modeling the likelihood to find a tomogram without a vesicle. A similar analysis of the cryo-CLEM of cells expressing mSc3-Sec9 estimated the fusion time to be 3.2 ± 1.1 seconds after Sec9 clustering which yields 6.2 ± 1.1 s after exocyst clustering. This result is in concordance with exocyst-based estimation given the relatively smaller sampling. Importantly, the lack of detected vesicles in our tomograms might happen when the ExHOS is captured in the lamella, but the vesicle is cut relatively peripherally. Thus, the missing wedge might hinder the vesicle detection resulting in “false negative” (i.e. tomograms correlated to diffraction-limited fluorescent clusters but devoid of vesicles because the vesicle detection is prevented by technical limitations). To estimate the upper limit for the fusion time, we assumed that all 19 tomograms devoid of vesicles in the exocyst-mNG dataset (19/95 = 20%) represent the maximum “false negative” rate of our approach. Under this assumption, only 6 of the 14 tomograms in the mSc3-Sec9 dataset would be really devoid of vesicles. Consequently, following the same approach as before, the fusion time would correspond to 8.1 ± 1.1 s after exocyst clustering. Per definition, a fusion time of 8.1 s after exocyst clustering implies that a dataset of 95 tomograms should have about 13 tomograms truly devoid of vesicles. Therefore, we used the fusion time estimated from the exocyst-mNG dataset for further analysis, as the assumption that all tomograms devoid of vesicles in the exocyst-mNG dataset are false negative overestimates the fusion time, while estimations based on small dataset as the mSc3-Sec9 might lack accuracy. Additionally, to model the continuous average vesicle approaching to the PM, we mapped the xth quantiles (x = 1/95,···,76/95) of the exocyst-mNG cryo-CLEM distances to the exocyst lifetime interval (0-9.4 s), (Figure 6D). An interval confidence of this approximation was estimated using a bootstrap strategy, i.e, by randomizing repeatedly the selected measured distances and reapplying the same quantile-to-time mapping. Integrative modelling of exocytosis We integrated key experimental data into a cohesive model of exocyst-mediated vesicle tethering in exocytosis (Figure 7; Video S1). This integrative model combines the continuous ExHOS conformational dynamics (Equation 2, based on SMLM-DL), the vesicle kinetics (Figure 6D, based on cryo-CLEM), the average radius of secretory vesicles (Figure 1A), the average stoichiometry of exocyst clusters and other proteins involved in exocytosis (Figures 1B, S1D, and S3A) and the clustering/disassembly of Sec2, Sec9 and Sec18 from live-cell imaging (Figures 3C and 3D). Modeling the yeast cis-SNARE complex The structure of the yeast cis-SNARE complex was predicted with AlphaFold3 Server86 using the fasta sequences of Sec9 (Uniprot87 ID P40357), Sso1 (Uniprot ID P32867) and Snc1 (Uniprot ID P31109) proteins. The top ranked prediction was used for analysis of the AlphaFold3 metrics86,88 and posterior visualization. Only the confident regions (pLDDT >70) were taken into account to represent the ribbon silhouette of the cis-SNARE complex (Figure S7A, top). Modeling the exocytic trans-SNARE complex Modeling of the trans-SNARE complex conformation was based on the mammalian trans-SNARE complex simulated previously.89 To identify the juxtamembrane linker (L) and the transmembrane region (TMR) of Sso1 and Snc1 proteins we performed a multiple sequence alignment with the mammalian homologs Syntaxin1 (Uniprot ID P32851) and Synaptobrevin2 (Uniprot ID P63045) (Figure S7A). The multiple sequence alignment was performed with Clustal Omega.90 We used MODELLER91 to predict, by comparative modeling, the yeast trans-SNARE complex using the simulated mammalian trans-SNARE complex as template structure. Finally, we used ChimeraX92 to represent the yeast trans-SNARE complex with a density map of 10 Å resolution (Figure S7A, bottom). Quantification and statistical analysis All particle tracking and SMLM experiments were acquired in three biological replicates. More detailed information regarding the number of replicates used in each experiment can be found in figure legends. Error bars in plots indicate the standard deviation (SD) unless otherwise indicated. To compare differences between groups, unpaired Student’s t-tests were performed using the SciPy package. Results were considered significant if p < 0.05. Significance levels are indicated as follows: not significant (ns), p-value < 0.05 (∗), p-value < 0.01 (∗∗), p-value < 0.001 (∗∗∗). enrichment.normalized_title: Continuum architecture dynamics of vesicle tethering in exocytosis
enrichment.normalized_summary: Data from complementary imaging techniques were integrated into a model that resolves the dynamic exocyst ensemble and membrane architecture during exocytosis, an essential cellular pathway. Sec18 mediates the rate of exocytosis by disassembling the exocyst higher-order structure after vesicle fusion.

articles.title: Structural decoding of reversible covalent linkage of odorants in human olfactory receptor OR6A2
articles.summary: The human olfactory receptor OR6A2, re-engineered to be functional, demonstrates the mechanism by which it detects aldehydes. Using this approach, Wang, Wu, et al. uncovered a broadly conserved activation switch in class II odorant receptors. This work also outlines a practical approach to decode smell, with potential uses in fragrance design and inflammation therapy.
articles.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Get Access Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • Cryo-EM structures of consOR6 reveal distinctive features of the OR6 subfamily • Back-mutated OR6A2 regains odorant responses seen in wild-type OR6A2 • Reversible covalent Schiff base linkages for odorants recognition are uncovered • A simplified activation mechanism and native Golf protein binding mode for ORs are elucidated Summary Olfactory receptors (ORs) are a diverse superfamily of G protein-coupled receptors responsible for odor detection that are also implicated in non-olfactory physiological functions. OR6A2, a class II OR, selectively senses medium-chain aldehydes and belongs to a cluster of ORs genetically associated with the “soapy” perception of cilantro. It also modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory responses. Structural studies of ORs have long been challenging. Using a back-mutation strategy, we engineered a functional OR6A2 variant (bmOR6A2) from a consensus OR6 (consOR6). Structures of bmOR6A2 in complex with aldehydes reveal a novel ligand-recognition mechanism involving a reversible Schiff base linkage with residue K4.60, validated by mass spectrometry. By integrating structures of consOR6, molecular dynamics simulations, and functional assays, we identified a conserved D45.51Y6.55Y7.41 triad critical for activation in class II ORs. These findings establish a practical strategy for decoding odorant recognition, offering new insights into olfaction signaling and applications in fragrance and therapeutic development. enrichment.normalized_title: Structural decoding of reversible covalent linkage of odorants in human olfactory receptor OR6A2
enrichment.normalized_summary: The human olfactory receptor OR6A2, re-engineered to be functional, demonstrates the mechanism by which it detects aldehydes. Using this approach, Wang, Wu, et al. uncovered a broadly conserved activation switch in class II odorant receptors. This work also outlines a practical approach to decode smell, with potential uses in fragrance design and inflammation therapy.

articles.title: MYC binding to nascent RNA suppresses innate immune signaling by R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids
articles.summary: RNA-binding-mediated multimerization of MYC concentrates RNA-degrading factors around double-stranded RNAs and R-loops. This prevents aberrant RNAs from accumulating and leaking into the cytosol. Through RNA binding, MYC suppresses innate immune signaling and promotes tumor growth.
articles.content: Skip to Main Content Skip to Main Menu Outline Download PDF Cite Share Set Alert Get Rights Reprints Previous article Next article Highlights • MYC is an RNA-binding protein that binds to nascent, intronic RNAs in cells • MYC moves from DNA to RNA under stress and multimerizes around dsRNAs and R-loops • MYC multimers concentrate RNA-degrading factors to limit the buildup of aberrant RNAs • RNA binding of MYC suppresses TLR3-pTBK1 signaling and promotes tumor development Summary In response to perturbed transcription elongation, the MYC oncoprotein multimerizes and undergoes a phase transition. Here, we demonstrate that MYC globally relocalizes from its canonical positions on DNA to nascent RNA upon accumulation of intronic RNA. Upon binding to RNA, MYC forms multimers that concentrate the nuclear exosome, an RNA exonuclease, and its targeting complexes around double-stranded RNA and R-loops. MYC harbors four RNA-binding regions (RBRI–IV). RBRIII promotes MYC multimerization and is necessary for recruiting the exosome to R-loops. RBRIII is dispensable for transcriptional activation and pancreatic tumor cell proliferation in culture, but it is indispensable for sustaining tumor growth in vivo. Via RBRIII, MYC suppresses the accumulation of R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids and prevents them from activating the innate immune kinase TBK1 via the TLR3 pattern recognition receptor. Our data demonstrate that the phase transition of MYC is an RNA-driven stress response that suppresses the accumulation of immunogenic RNA-DNA hybrids. Graphical abstract Keywords MYC RNA binding TLR3 TBK1 R-loop exosome innate immune signaling pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma PDAC Introduction The MYC protein is an oncogenic driver in many tumor entities.1 Relative to normal tissues, MYC expression is enhanced in human tumors due to mutations in the MYC gene or as a downstream consequence of a plethora of alterations in signaling pathways that collectively control MYC expression. Wherever tested, tumors depend on elevated MYC expression throughout their lifetime, prompting numerous attempts to target MYC for tumor therapy.2,3 MYC forms a DNA-binding complex with MAX that associates with most active promoters and enhancers.4,5 The complex exerts both positive and, in conjunction with additional partner proteins, negative effects on the expression of large sets of genes, resulting in a characteristic expression profile of MYC-driven tumors.4,5 Increased MYC expression stimulates cell growth and proliferation and reprograms cellular metabolism. These cell-autonomous effects correlate with the altered expression of the respective MYC target genes.5 However, not all oncogenic effects of MYC can be explained by changes in gene expression.6 For example, MYC establishes an immunologically “cold” microenvironment and allows tumors to escape from immune surveillance.7,8,9,10 Depletion of MYC in a p53/KRAS-driven (“KPC”) model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)11 results in tumor regression in immunocompetent mice but has little effect when cells are transplanted into immunodeficient mice.12,13 Mechanistically, MYC suppresses the activity of the TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), which activates nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) and interferon-dependent genes.13,14 Deletion of TBK1 abrogates the dependence of tumor growth on MYC, demonstrating that suppression of TBK1 is the critical function of MYC in this model.12 Activation of TBK1 in MYC-depleted cells depends on Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3), a pattern recognition receptor,12 which recognizes double-stranded (ds)RNA and RNA-DNA hybrids derived from nuclear R-loops,15,16 arguing that MYC suppresses their accumulation on TLR3 and that this is critical for its oncogenic function. Consistently, MYC represses the transcription of genes that are required for TLR3 function,8,12 but whether MYC directly affects dsRNA or R-loop metabolism is unknown. Both MYC and MYCN directly bind RNA in addition to DNA.17,18,19 In MYC, a short motif (KRR), which is contained in the basic region, interacts with both DNA and RNA and enhances MYC binding to promoters and transcriptional activation of its target genes.19 MYCN harbors a distinct RNA-binding domain in the amino terminus, which is not required for transcriptional activation.17 Rather, MYCN binds RNA as part of the nuclear exosome targeting (NEXT) complex, which targets the nuclear exosome to non-polyadenylated RNAs and promotes the degradation of intron-derived nascent RNAs.20 In MYCN-driven neuroblastoma cells, MYCN RNA binding enhances stress resilience during S-phase, suggesting that it attenuates transcriptional activation in response to transcriptional or replication stress.17,20 A fraction of MYC exists in a multimeric state, and perturbing transcription elongation by inhibition of the spliceosome or the FACT (facilitates chromatin transcription) histone chaperone causes MYC proteins to undergo a phase transition and form large sphere-like structures.21 This transition has little effect on gene expression but protects stalled replication forks from RNA polymerase and prevents transcription-replication conflicts.21 Here, we show that MYC multimerization reflects the transition from a DNA- to an RNA-bound form of MYC. MYC harbors four RNA-binding regions (RBRs), of which RBRIII has no role in transcriptional activation by MYC. Rather, RBRIII promotes MYC multimerization and the recruitment of the nuclear exosome to R-loops. In pancreatic tumor cells, RBRIII suppresses the activation of TBK1 by RNA-DNA hybrids that are derived from nuclear MYC-bound R-loops, directly linking RNA binding of MYC to its ability to suppress innate immune signaling. Results MYC binds nascent RNA To investigate whether MYC is bound to RNA in cells, we performed cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) experiments in K562 chronic myeloid leukemia cells, which express elevated levels of MYC.22 SDS-PAGE of immunoprecipitations (IPs) of MYC from UV-crosslinked cells stained positive for RNA, with the signal being sensitive to RNase I (Figure 1A). Control immunoglobulin G (IgG)-IPs and MYC-IPs from cells that were not UV-cross-linked contained no RNA, confirming the specificity of the signal. Analysis of single-end enhanced CLIP (seCLIP) sequencing23 of immunoprecipitated RNA identified 11,077 reproducible enriched windows in MYC-IPs versus 72 reproducible enriched windows in IgG controls using the Skipper algorithm24 (Figure 1B). Heatmaps as well as inspection of individual genes confirmed the specificity of the MYC signal (Figures 1C and 1D). Around 70% of MYC-bound sites were localized in intronic RNA, and about 10% were adjacent to splice sites, indicating that MYC binds to nascent or unprocessed transcripts, consistent with findings for MYCN17 (Figure 1E). Normalizing the number of MYC-bound sequence windows to the total number of windows assigned to different RNA features revealed that MYC RNA binding is distributed evenly across multiple sequence elements (Figure S1A). Direct comparisons suggested that the promoter-distal RNA-binding sites of MYC were not identified in previous analyses mainly due to the use of MACS2, an algorithm developed for identifying short binding sites on chromatin.19 The distribution of MYC binding sites was similar to that of other intron-binding proteins (Figure S1B). Many introns contained multiple MYC-bound windows, suggesting that individual introns are potentially bound by multiple MYC molecules (Figure S1C). GO term analysis did not reveal any enrichment of a functional class of transcripts among MYC-bound genes. De novo motif analysis of MYC-bound RNA windows using either the Skipper or the PureCLIP25 algorithm showed a moderate enrichment of several UG-rich motifs (Figure S1D), similar to MYCN RNA binding.17 MYC RNA-binding sites were not enriched for E-box sequences, to which MYC/MAX complexes bind on DNA. A comparison with MYC ChIP-sequencing data revealed the co-existence of genes with MYC binding at the promoters, those with MYC binding to nascent RNA, and those with both DNA and RNA MYC binding. Consistently, quantitative analyses showed that the amount of MYC bound to each mRNA was not correlated with the amount of MYC bound to its promoter (Figure S1E), arguing that binding of MYC to promoters and to nascent RNA are independent of each other. We also performed seCLIP experiments in U2OS expressing doxycycline-inducible ectopic MYC (U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells). U2OS cells express 1.8 × 105 endogenous MYC molecules per cell,21 which is comparable to proliferating non-transformed cells and lower than those found in many tumor cell lines.26 In EtOH-treated U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells, the overall binding of endogenous MYC to RNA was very similar to that observed in K562 cells: Skipper identified 3,220 reproducible enriched windows, with MYC binding being predominantly intronic (Figures S1F and S1G). Figure 1 MYC binds to nascent RNA Show full caption Figure S1 Characterization of MYC RNA binding, related to Figure 1 Show full caption Fractionation of U2OS cells into chromatin, nucleoplasm, and cytosol before performing eCLIP experiments showed that there are both chromatin-associated and nucleoplasmic pools of MYC (Figure 1F). MYC and other soluble nuclear proteins were also detected in the cytosol, likely due to leakage during fractionation. MYC-bound RNA was found almost exclusively in the chromatin fraction (Figures 1G and S2A). Like total MYC, chromatin-associated MYC was largely bound to intronic RNA (Figure S2B). To test whether MYC binds RNA during or immediately after transcription, we performed eCLIP experiments on cells treated for 1 h with NVP-2, a specific inhibitor of CDK9 that blocks RNAPII pause release.27 Since the MYC mRNA is highly unstable, we performed these experiments in U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells that had been treated with doxycycline for 24 h. Under these conditions, U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells express approximately 3 × 106 molecules of MYC per cell, about three-fold higher than MYC levels in colon carcinoma26 and glioblastoma cells.28 CLIP experiments revealed an increase in MYC RNA binding upon doxycycline induction that paralleled the increase in MYC protein levels (Figures S2C and S2D). The overall binding pattern of MYC to RNA was very similar between low and elevated MYC levels (Figure S2E). Skipper analyses revealed a two-fold increase in the overall number of MYC binding sites on RNA. While binding to introns was largely conserved between low and elevated MYC levels, elevated MYC levels showed enhanced binding to exons (Figures S2F and S2G). Inhibition of CDK9 with NVP-2 for 1 h caused a strong decrease in RNA binding of MYC (Figure 2A), while total MYC levels were unaffected (Figures S2H and S2I). For each RNA, the decrease in MYC binding paralleled the decrease in abundance and was more pronounced for introns than for exons, suggesting that it is due to the processing of RNA (Figures 2B and 2C). We concluded that MYC binds chromatin-associated nascent RNA during or shortly after transcription. Figure 2 RNA- and DNA-bound pools of MYC are in a dynamic equilibrium Show full caption Figure S2 Additional characterization of MYC RNA binding, related to Figures 1 and 2 Show full caption MYC proteins exist in a dynamic equilibrium of DNA- and RNA-bound pools In response to inhibition of the FACT histone chaperone or the SF3B1 subunit of the spliceosome, MYC proteins undergo a phase transition and multimerize,21 prompting us to investigate whether inhibition of FACT or the spliceosome affects the distribution of MYC between RNA- and DNA-bound pools. To address these questions, we performed parallel chromatin-immunoprecipitation (ChIP) sequencing for MYC and RNAPII and seCLIP sequencing of doxycycline-treated U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells that had been treated with the FACT inhibitor CBL0137.29 Exposure to CBL0137 strongly increased both the overall number of MYC RNA-binding sites and binding of MYC to many individual sites (Figures 2D–2F). The majority of the CBL0137-specific binding sites were intronic, suggesting that FACT blockade increases MYC occupancy at unprocessed transcripts (Figure 2G). Accordingly, CBL0137 treatment led to a relative increase in the number of intronic RNAs being present in the input of seCLIP experiments (Figure S3A). ChIP-Rx sequencing showed that CBL0137 caused a strong decrease of RNAPII chromatin occupancy close to promoters and a decrease in pS2-phosphorylated elongating RNAPII (RNAPIIpS2) in gene bodies, which is most likely due to both transcription termination30,31 and degradation of RNAPII,32 suggesting that MYC binds nascent RNA that is released from RNAPII in CBL0137-treated cells (Figures S3B and S3C). Figure S3 CBL0137- and PlaB-dependent changes in transcription elongation and MYC RNA binding, related to Figure 2 Show full caption MYC binding to several individual E-box-containing promoters decreases upon FACT inhibition.21 ChIP-Rx sequencing from doxycycline-treated U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells showed that FACT inhibition caused a virtually complete loss of chromatin-bound MYC from active promoters (Figure 2H). Similarly, inhibition of the spliceosome factor, SF3B1, by pladienolide B (PlaB) caused a global redistribution of MYC from active promoters to intronic RNA (Figures S3D and S3E), with many RNA-binding sites proximal to splice sites (Figure S3F). Since spliceosome inhibition delays transcription elongation, which is reflected by an increase of promoter-proximal relative to elongating RNAPII33 (Figures S3B and S3C), and causes an increase in unprocessed RNAs,34,35 we hypothesized that the increase in MYC RNA binding is due to the accumulation of intronic RNAs. To test this, we used small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to deplete EXOSC5, a core subunit of the nuclear exosome, which degrades intronic RNAs.36 seCLIP experiments revealed that depletion of EXOSC5 caused an increase in MYC RNA binding (Figures S3G and S3H), which was reflected in the increased total levels of many intronic RNAs. Parallel experiments performed in cells treated with siRNA targeting MYC confirmed the specificity of the signal (Figures S3G and S3H). We concluded that accumulation of intronic RNAs shifts MYC from a DNA-bound to an RNA-bound state. MYC multimers co-localize with RNA-degrading factors around R-loops and dsRNA Blocking nascent transcription by the CDK9 inhibitor NVP-2 shortly before FACT inhibition decreased the number of MYC multimers despite unaltered MYC levels, suggesting that multimers form around nascent RNA (Figure S4A). We therefore tested whether MYC associates with RNA metabolizing or degrading factors (Figure 3A). IP of MYC in U2OS cells co-immunoprecipitated MAX as well as total RNAPII and elongating RNAPIIpS2 (Figure 3A). Anti-MYC, but not control IPs, also contained EXOSC10, a catalytic subunit of the exosome; ZCCHC8, the scaffolding subunit of the NEXT complex; YTHDC1, RBM15, and METTL3, which are involved in m6A metabolism; and the RNA-binding proteins FUS, HNRNPC, and STRBP (Figure 3A). In these experiments, we added an RNase inhibitor to the lysate. Treatment of cell lysates with benzonase, which degrades both DNA and RNA, had no effect on the interaction of MYC with multiple RNA-degrading factors, ruling out that they were mediated indirectly via binding to RNA (Figure S4B). Reverse co-IPs confirmed the interactions of MYC with several RNA processing factors (Figure S4C). Treatment of cells with MG-132 or CBL0137, both of which induce MYC multimerization,21 caused changes in the amount of co-immunoprecipitating proteins that paralleled overall changes in MYC levels, arguing that MYC binds to these proteins constitutively (Figure S4D). Quantitative immunofluorescence experiments from doxycycline-treated U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells that had been exposed to CBL0137 showed that multiple factors involved in RNA metabolism and degradation were concentrated in MYC multimers (Figure 3B). On average, 10% of the total MYC protein was concentrated in foci, whereas the values for co-localizing proteins were always lower than the MYC values, ranging from 1.6% (MTR4) to 8.8% (EXOSC10) (Figure S4E). By contrast, the ARS2 protein, which binds to nascent mRNA; the INTS11 and ZC3H4 subunits of integrator and restrictor transcription termination complexes; CPSF3, which is a subunit of the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity complex; and Hexim1, which is a negative regulator of RNAPII pause release, did not localize to MYC multimers (Figure S4F). Figure 3 MYC multimers are hubs of RNA degradation and processing factors Show full caption Figure S4 Additional analysis of MYC protein interactions, related to Figure 3 Show full caption To determine whether specific RNA structures are localized within MYC multimers, we stained cells with J2, a monoclonal antibody that recognizes dsRNA. In addition, we stably expressed the hybrid-binding domain (HBD) of RNase H1, which recognizes RNA-DNA hybrids, fused to an antibody tag, using a mutant allele (“WKK”) that carries three point mutations in the HBD (WKK) as specificity control (Figure S5A). In doxycycline-treated U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells, both dsRNA and R-loops were concentrated in MYC multimers in the presence of CBL0137 (Figures 3C and 3D). Consistently, RNA-DNA IP followed by cDNA conversion (DRIPc) sequencing, which maps the genome-wide distribution of R-loops, showed no significant enrichment of R-loops at MYC-bound RNAs in control cells, while R-loops identified in CBL0137-treated cells overlapped with MYC RNA-binding sites (Figures S5B–S5D). To determine whether the presence of R-loops or R-loop-mediated transcription-replication conflicts is required for MYC multimerization, we stably expressed RNase H1 fused to a nuclear-localization signal in U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells and confirmed that the enzyme localizes to the nucleus (Figure S5E). Parallel measurements of MYC levels and number of multimeric foci showed that expression of RNase H1 attenuated MYC multimerization in response to CBL0137 (Figure S5F). Independent quantitation of the MYC immunofluorescence signal and the number of foci in more than 3,000 cells showed that removing R-loops decreased MYC multimerization independent of MYC levels (Figure 3E). We concluded that MYC multimers form hubs that concentrate RNA degradation in the vicinity of R-loops and dsRNA and that R-loops promote multimerization of MYC. Figure S5 Analyses of R-loops in the context of MYC multimers, related to Figure 3 Show full caption Failure to degrade nascent RNA drives MYC multimerization To pinpoint the factors that drive MYC multimerization, we screened 84 siRNAs that target proteins contained in the interactome of MYC multimers21 or RNA-bound MYCN16 (Figure S5G). We transfected U2OSMYC-Tet-On cells that had been treated with doxycycline to minimize effects on MYC expression with specific siRNAs and measured their effect on MYC multimer formation. As controls, we confirmed that siRNAs targeting SUPTH16 and SSRP1, two subunits of the FACT complex targeted by CBL0137, and SF3B1, the spliceosome subunit targeted by pladienolide B, promoted MYC multimerization (Figure S5H).21 The results showed that siRNAs targeting RNA processing and degrading factors induced MYC multimerization in unstressed cells (Figures 3F and 3G). A second siRNA screen depleting subunits of the nuclear exosome and its targeting complexes, TRAMP, NEXT, and PAXT, as well as additional factors, such as ARS2,37 showed that depletion of subunits of the exosome and the NEXT complex, which targets the exosome to degrade non-polyadenylated RNAs, triggered MYC multimerization, whereas depletion of other factors had weak or no effects (Figures S5I and S5J). Upon FACT inhibition, MYC multimerizes close to stalled replication forks,21 and the same occurs upon depletion of several exosome subunits, the NEXT subunit ZCCHC8, and other RNA-degrading factors (Figures S5K and S5L). Notably, MYC RNA-binding sites showed a significant overlap with EXOSC10 binding sites (Figure 3H). We concluded that failure to degrade nascent or aberrant RNAs stabilizes MYC multimers. MYC is a multivalent RNA-binding protein To understand whether MYC binds RNA directly, we purified recombinant, full-length (FL) MYC protein (Figure S6A). Incubation of MYC with two single-stranded (ss)RNA oligonucleotides corresponding to intronic RNA sites that are strongly bound by MYC in seCLIP experiments (PTDSS2 and ANKRD11) revealed similar affinities and apparent Kd values of 0.22 ± 0.04 μM for PTDSS2 RNA and 0.72 ± 0.16 μM for the ANKRD11 RNA. The latter harbors a UUAGUAG motif identified in the PureCLIP analyses described above (Figure S6B). These values are similar to recently published affinities of MYC to G-rich RNA sequences.19 Consistent with multiple previous data showing that MYC binding to E-boxes requires heterodimerization with MAX,1,4 MYC did not show a high affinity to either ssDNA or dsDNA that contain a consensus E-box sequence (Figure S6C). MYC also had low affinities to RNA contained in an RNA-DNA hybrid and to dsRNA (Figure S6C). MYC co-localization with these structures in cells may be promoted by MYC’s association with the MTR4 helicase of the NEXT complex or senataxin (Figure 3B).17,38 Figure S6 Further characterization of MYC multimerization and RNA binding in vitro and in cells, related to Figure 4 Show full caption To identify the residues that mediate RNA binding, we used peptide libraries consisting of overlapping 25mer peptides spanning the entire MYC sequence. This analysis identified four RBRs (“RBRI–IV”), with RBRIII, which surrounds MYCBox IV,39 showing the strongest binding (Figure 4A). RBRIV comprises the basic region that binds DNA and that contains an arginine-rich RNA-binding motif that enhances the interaction of MYC with promoters.19 To identify additional roles of MYC RNA binding, we performed fluorescence anisotropy assays and found that recombinant proteins encompassing amino acids (aa) 1–163 and aa 304–354 showed significant affinity to ssRNA with apparent Kd values of 1.94 ± 0.24 and 1.92 ± 0.24 μM, respectively (Figures 4D and S6D).17 Since the RBRs overlap with sequences involved in protein modification and turnover, we stably expressed several alleles in which basic residues in these domains had been replaced by alanine (Figure S6E) in U2OS cells, in which the endogenous MYC gene has been tagged with an auxin-inducible degron (U2OSMYC-AID cells).21 All amino-terminal replacement mutants were expressed at significantly lower levels than wild-type MYC (WTMYC), precluding their further analysis in cells (Figures S6F and S6G). By contrast, a mutant allele carrying six alanine replacements in RBRIII (K316A, K317A, R331A, R334A, R340A, and K341A) was expressed at the same level as WTMYC (Figures 4B, 4C, and S6F). In vitro binding assays confirmed that these mutations abolished RNA binding (Figure 4D), and we therefore performed subsequent assays with this allele (RBRIIIMUTMYC). RBRIIIMUTMYC retains the HCF-1 binding site39 in MYCBox IV and three basic aa (K323, R324, and K326) that are part of the nuclear-localization signal and was exclusively localized in the nucleus (Figures 4B and S6H).40 eCLIP sequencing revealed that the ability of RBRIIIMUTMYC to bind nascent RNA cells was significantly impaired relative to WTMYC, as seen on multiple individual RNAs and reflected by the decreased overall number of RNA-binding sites in RBRIIIMUTMYC-expressing cells treated with CBL0137 (Figures 4E and 4F). In parallel ChIP-Rx sequencing experiments, the association of RBRIIIMUTMYC with promoter-proximal chromatin was virtually indistinguishable from WTMYC in unstressed cells (Figures 4G, 4H, and 4I). Both WTMYC and RBRIIIMUTMYC chromatin binding sites were highly enriched in the E-box sequences that are the consensus DNA-binding motif of MYC/MAX complexes (Figure S6I). In contrast to WTMYC, RBRIIIMUTMYC was partially retained on chromatin following CBL0137 treatment, demonstrating that the relocalization of MYC from DNA onto nascent RNA requires an intact RBRIII (Figures 4H and 4I). RBRIIIMUTMYC was impaired in its ability to form multimers in cells, arguing that MYC multimers form around RNA (Figures 4J, 4K, and S6J). In vitro, fluorescently labeled RNA was recruited into droplets formed by recombinant MYC proteins21 (Figure S7A), and incubation with an ssRNA oligonucleotide enhanced MYC multimerization in an RNase A-sensitive manner (Figure S7B), suggesting that RNA promotes MYC multimerization in part via a direct interaction. Upon exposure of U2OS cells to CBL0137, RBRIIIMUTMYC was impaired in its ability to co-localize with EXOSC10 relative to WTMYC (Figures 4K and 4L). Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) showed that endogenous MYC promotes the recruitment of EXOSC10 to R-loops (Figure S7C) and that RBRIIIMUTMYC is impaired in the ability to recruit EXOSC10 to R-loops (Figures 4M and 4N). Figure 4 MYC is a multivalent RNA-binding protein Show full caption Figure S7 Further characterization of the MYC RBR mutants, related to Figures 4, 5, 6, and 7 Show full caption RBRIII of MYC is required to suppress innate immune signaling In response to stress, MYC multimers accumulate in normal and tumor cell lines and in human multiple myeloma patient samples (Figure S7D).21 MYC-MYC and MYC-MAX PLAs in human colon tumors and adjacent normal tissue (Figures 5A and S7E) revealed that MYC/MAX heterodimers were present at similar levels in both normal and tumor tissue. By contrast, MYC multimers were virtually undetectable in normal tissue, but their levels greatly increased in tumors. We also detected MYC multimers in human pancreatic cancer tissue samples (Figures 5B and S7F). Figure 5 RNA binding of MYC suppresses innate immune signaling in PDAC cells and promotes tumor growth in vivo Show full caption To explore whether RNA binding via RBRIII and the formation of multimers confers a selective advantage to tumor cells, we expressed WTMYC and RBRIIIMUTMYC in pancreatic KPC cells expressing doxycycline-inducible short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting endogenous MYC.12,13 Immunoblots confirmed the depletion of endogenous MYC upon doxycycline addition and showed that WTMYC and RBRIIIMUTMYC were expressed at equal levels (Figure 5C). As observed in U2OS cells, eCLIP experiments showed that RBRIIIMUTMYC was impaired in binding to nascent and intronic RNAs (Figures 5D and 5E), while parallel ChIP-Rx sequencing experiments showed that its association with promoter-proximal chromatin was virtually identical to WTMYC (Figures 5F, 5G, and 5H). Expression of both WTMYC and, to a slightly lesser extent, RBRIIIMUTMYC stimulated the proliferation of KPC cells in culture (Figure 5I). Next, we transplanted tumor cells that stably express firefly luciferase orthotopically into C57BL/6 syngeneic mice. After 7 days, we added doxycycline to deplete endogenous MYC and induce the expression of either WTMYC or RBRIIIMUTMYC. In these experiments, tumors expressing WTMYC exhibited on average a 24-fold increase in size over 28 days, while those expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC showed a 94% reduction in volume during the same period (Figures 5J and 5K), demonstrating that RBRIII is largely dispensable in culture but required to prevent tumor regression in vivo. To understand this phenotype, we performed RNA sequencing of cells treated with doxycycline for 48 h, and this showed that WTMYC and RBRIIIMUTMYC were indistinguishable in their ability to activate canonical MYC target gene sets and E2F-dependent genes involved in cell cycle progression (Figure 5L). By contrast, while WTMYC also repressed genes driven by multiple transcription factors involved in innate immune signaling, including NF-kB/RelA, retinoic acid receptor, and interferon-regulatory factor (Irf1), RBRIIIMUTMYC was impaired in repressing these gene sets (Figure 5L). Since both NF-kB and IRF-dependent transcription are activated by TBK1, the differences in gene expression may reflect the failure of RBRIIIMUTMYC to suppress TBK1 activity. In strong support of this hypothesis, RBRIIIMUTMYC was unable to suppress TBK1 autophosphorylation, a hallmark of active TBK1,41 as well as P62 phosphorylation42 and LC3 lipidation,43 downstream targets of TBK1 (Figure 5C). RBRIII of MYC is required for R-loop binding and suppression of DNA/RNA hybrids Activation of TBK1 upon depletion of MYC depends on the pattern recognition receptor TLR3, which binds both dsRNA and R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids.12,16,44 PLAs measuring the proximity of TRIF1, a substrate adaptor protein, to TLR3 yielded a strong signal in MYC-depleted cells, which was suppressed by expression of WTMYC but to a much lesser degree by RBRIIIMUTMYC (Figure 6A). seCLIP experiments showed that TLR3 bound to both coding RNAs and several classes of non-coding RNAs and that the number of enriched RNAs increased for several RNA classes after depletion of MYC (Figures 6B and 6C). MYC depletion also increased the number of TLR3-bound RNAs that were localized to R-loops as determined by DRIPc sequencing (Figure 6D). PLA assays showed that RBRIIIMUTMYC, like WTMYC, suppressed dsRNA loading on TLR3 (Figure 6E), which is consistent with the finding that the number of repetitive elements bound by WTMYC or RBRIIIMUTMYC was unaltered as assessed by eCLIP sequencing (Figure S7G). In contrast to WTMYC, RBRIIIMUTMYC was unable to prevent the accumulation of RNA-DNA hybrids on TLR3 (Figure 6F), arguing that RBRIII functions in R-loop metabolism. PLAs with the RIG-I, MDA5, and cGAS pattern recognition receptors showed similar but much weaker effects (Figures S7H and S7I). Figure 6 MYC RNA binding suppresses the accumulation of RNA-DNA hybrids on TLR3 Show full caption Compared with WTMYC, RBRIIIMUTMYC showed reduced proximity and interaction with R-loops in KPC cells (Figures 7A and S7J), prompting us to map R-loops in MYC-depleted cells and cells expressing WTMYC or RBRIIIMUTMYC. These assays identified 4,912 R-loop regions, 501 of which were localized in genes with MYC-bound RNAs (Figure 7B). The majority of these R-loops were located in introns (Figure 7C). Quantification of the DRIPc signal within the 501 MYC RNA-bound genes showed that the amount of RNA contained in R-loops was significantly higher in cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC than in cells expressing WTMYC (Figure 7D). RBRIIIMUTMYC did not alter the expression of the genes that harbor these R-loops relative to WTMYC, demonstrating that the increase in R-loop abundance is independent of expression differences in the host genes (Figure 7E). The amount of RBRIIIMUTMYC bound to RNAs contained in R-loops was significantly lower than that of WTMYC (Figure 7F). Examination of individual genes identified several examples of MYC-bound R-loops that accumulate in cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC but not in cells expressing WTMYC and showed that the RNA contained in these R-loops is bound by TLR3 upon MYC depletion (Figure 7G). RNA levels in MYC-bound R-loops increased significantly upon EXOSC10 depletion, with the increase being more pronounced on MYC-bound genes compared with all R-loop-containing genes (Figures 7G and 7H). While KPC cells expressing WTMYC displayed low basal levels of R-loops at multiple genes that were enhanced upon EXOSC10 depletion, KPC cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC showed high basal levels of R-loops, which were not further enhanced by EXOSC10 depletion, arguing that MYC and EXOSC10 cooperate to suppress R-loop accumulation (Figures 7I and 7J). Collectively, our data show that MYC, via RBRIII, recruits the RNA exosome to suppress loading of both dsRNA and R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids onto TLR3. Figure 7 TLR3-bound RNA-DNA hybrids are derived from nuclear R-loops bound by MYC Show full caption Discussion Here, we demonstrate that the MYC protein is a multivalent RNA-binding protein that harbors four RBRs (RBRI–IV). Of these, RBRIV corresponds to the basic region, which also binds DNA.19 The three additional RBRs overlap with evolutionary highly conserved domains termed “MYCBoxes.”6 MYC binds broadly to nascent and intronic RNAs independently of DNA binding at promoters, and mutation of RBRIII compromises this ability. In cells, MYC globally relocalizes from DNA to nascent RNA when RNA processing or transcriptional elongation is perturbed. Stress conditions that enhance MYC RNA binding coincide with the formation of MYC multimers with condensate-like properties.21,45,46 Point mutations that disable RNA binding by RBRIII or the removal of RNA-DNA hybrids by the ectopic expression of RNase H1 compromise the ability of MYC to multimerize in cells, arguing that MYC binding to RNA promotes multimerization. Most likely, MYC multimerization involves the binding of multiple MYC molecules to the same or adjacent RNA molecules, similar to other RNA-protein interactions that compartmentalize RNA metabolic processes.47 Since MYC proteins form droplet-like condensates,21,46 and incubation with RNA moderately enhances condensate formation in vitro, MYC proteins are also likely to have an inherent capacity to multimerize, which is enhanced by their interaction with RNA or other RNA-binding proteins. MYC multimers concentrate the nuclear exosome, a 3′–5′ RNA exonuclease complex, and its targeting complexes around dsRNA and R-loops, arguing that MYC multimers compartmentalize the nuclear RNA degradation machinery. RBRIIIMUTMYC shows reduced binding to multiple introns that can harbor R-loops. In PDAC cells, RNA-DNA hybrids from these R-loops accumulate in cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC, but not in cells expressing WTMYC. To suppress RNA-DNA hybrid accumulation, MYC recruits the nuclear exosome to RNA sequences that otherwise form RNA-DNA hybrids and R-loops. In PDACs, RBRIIIMUTMYC promotes cell proliferation in culture but is deficient in sustaining tumor growth in vivo, arguing that RBRIII contributes a critical function to tumorigenesis. MYC suppresses the accumulation of both dsRNAs and R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids on TLR3, which recognizes both nucleic acid species.16,48 While RBRIIIMUTMYC retains the ability to suppress dsRNA accumulation on TLR3, a class of MYC-bound, intron-derived R-loops accumulates on TLR3, and TBK1 is highly active in cells expressing RBRIIIMUTMYC. R-loops can be cleaved from the genome, and R-loop-derived RNA-DNA hybrids can be exported from the nucleus to activate TLR3.16 We propose that RNA binding by RBRIII is critical in tumors since it enables MYC to suppress the accumulation of RNA-DNA hybrids on TLR3, downstream TBK1 activation, and the subsequent TBK1-dependent eradication of tumor cells by the immune system.12 Our data establish that MYC has mechanistically distinct functions in transcription and RNA metabolism. While MYC multimers21 and RNA-bound pools of MYC are detectable in unstressed cells, levels of both greatly increase in response to transcriptional stress. Intriguingly, MYC multimers are present in human colon tumors and PDACs, and depletion of MYC in PDAC cells increases the accumulation of misprocessed RNAs and R-loops in the absence of exogenous stress. Both observations suggest that tumor cells experience endogenous stresses, such as transcription-replication conflicts, that perturb transcription elongation. MYC mutants that are unable to bind RNA retain their mitogenic potential, suggesting that they maintain physiological functions. We therefore propose that targeting the ability of MYC to bind RNA will disrupt the immune-evasive functions of MYC and open a wide therapeutic window. Limitations of the study While RBRIIIMUTMYC shows a substantial decrease in RNA binding, it is not completely deficient, suggesting that other RBRs contribute to RNA binding in cells. Hence, the functions of RNA-bound MYC may extend beyond R-loop metabolism. The mechanisms by which RNA-DNA hybrids are excised from chromatin and exported to the cytosol and how the tumor microenvironment is shaped by RNA binding of the MYC remain to be clarified. Finally, the role of RNA binding in MYC-driven oncogenesis likely differs between tumor entities.
